speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek consent of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43 in a case of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the continued inactivity on the part of the government, making ineffectual the administration of the Combines Investigation Branch in one way by keeping the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission without a chairman since May, 1970, and with only one member since the end of December last year. subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. Prime Minister. What is the position of his government now with regard to the receipts of the oil producing provinces, the proportion of the export tax that may be paid to oil producing provinces? Is the position of the government today that this is subject to equalization, or not?

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question is part of a whole series of questions that I am in the process of discussing with the premiers of the oil producing provinces and of the oil consuming provinces. We have a position on this point and I have put it to the premiers. I would hesitate to state it now because it is part of a package, I repeat, which we are negotiating with the provinces which have opposing interests. I would be reluctant, indeed, to have to indicate at this stage of the negotiations what the government's position is.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister and I am not really asking him for a legal opinion. In view of the position taken prior to the recess of the House that the share of the export tax received by the oil producing provinces was subject to equalization, and specific sums were actually mentioned as to what would have to be paid with respect to equalization for the months of September, October, November and December, and in view of the indication by the Minister of Finance since then that, technically speaking at least, a proportion of the export tax received by the oil producing provinces was not subject to equalization, I should like to ask the Prime Minister not what his package is-I am not inquiring about his package for discussion-but whether it is his position that his government is bound under the existing law to regard those moneys received by these oil producing provinces to date as subject to equalization?

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. Leader of the Opposition is talking about the past, the opinion expressed by the Minister of Finance is one we stand by, that is, to the effect that these amounts are not subject to equalization.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: If that is the present position of the government, that these payments are not subject to equalization, can the Prime Minister explain why the government told the House, when the export tax matter was before the House for legislative purposes prior to the recess, that these payments were subject to equalization?

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my recollection of what we told the House is that the receiving provinces under the equalization system had benefited largely in the past year, notably by the increases announced by the Minister of Finance last spring, and that the provinces therefore were in a better position with regard to equalization than they had been in previous years. It is true that I remember indicating that they probably would benefit from the increased returns to the oil producing provinces, and that still remains the case. subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration; I am glad to see him back. Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment yesterday I had made some remarks with respect to matters of a local nature that are of concern to the government and matters of concern to the government nationally. I would now like to comment briefly on some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Saint-Hya-cinthe (Mr. Wagner), whose speech I listened to yesterday with great interest. He referred to a story during his speech. My recollection of that story is that it had its origin with an Irish Boston politician who said, "These are my principles and policies and if you don't like them- well, I have others."
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe entered the House with a reputation, unexcelled by any other member, for his commitment to law and order as a prosecutor, as a judge, and as a minister of justice for the province of Quebec. However, it was not long before he, like the Irish Boston politician, reverted to other policies and principles.
Both in the House and in committee he supported the 90-day notice provision inserted in the Protection of Privacy Act which provision, I fear, will greatly restrict the investigative powers of the police in their efforts to control criminal activity. In his speech the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe also made reference to what he termed "the Liberal-NDP charade." May I point out that the NDP support has been for good Liberal policies which have resulted in good laws for Canada-some 50 pieces of good legislation.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of equal significance is the fact that when the Conservative opposition joined with the New Democratic party, for whatever reasons, the product of that union was the 90-day notice provision which in fact places a fire alarm bell in the offices of organized crime, warning them that law enforcement agencies are investigating their criminal activities. The result of that union produced an illegitimate section in what is otherwise a worth-while piece of legislation.
However, Mr. Speaker, I must agree with the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe when he says that politics, if they are to have any meaning today, must be synonymous with integrity, honesty and responsive government. The word "politics" has gained many unsavoury connotations in recent months. The events surrounding Watergate in the United States have had a deep effect on the faith of the American people in their government, on the integrity of politics, and on the credibility of politicians in general. These effects have spilled over into Canada.
We all have a responsibility to restore politics to its place as a respectable and respected profession in the eyes of the public. Politicians themselves must ensure that they
The Address-Mr. Poulin
are honest, not only in fact but in every facet of the appearance of their actions. The fact that the authority of the government is no longer automatically accepted, especially by younger people, is not in itself an unhealthy attitude if it results in people taking a more active interest in their government.
There is another area of concern to me on which the throne speech was silent. I had hoped that included in it would be an announcement of forthcoming changes in the Narcotic Control Act regarding commercial trafficking in heroin and other similar hard drugs. This is an area which is becoming more and more of a concern to Canadians. The illicit commercial trafficking in hard drugs is becoming more and more of a threat to the health and well-being of Canadians. This problem continues to grow and is one of the major social concerns facing our nation.
My research indicates that the domestic illicit heroin problem is the most serious of our multi-drug problems. The number of persons addicted to heroin in Canada has continued to increase. It is now estimated that there are between 16,000 and 19,000 persons using this drug in our country. If we go back in the chain of supply, inevitably we must find that those who are using heroin, and who are the unfortunate captives of this addictive habit, have been supplied with their drug, and in many cases induced to become users of it, by those whom I would term commercial traffickers in heroin.
For purposes only of my remarks at this time, Mr. Speaker, I would define a commercial trafficker in heroin as one who sells a quantity of heroin, for example, 250 grams, which is equal to eight ounces or half a pound and has a current street value of $100,000. Such traffickers are clearly and without doubt in this most reprehensible criminal activity for the sole motive of profit, greed and avarice. Such traffickers stand to double or triple their investment and we can easily see that the profits are indeed high. I believe that we must impose the most severe and stringent sanctions on such criminal activity so that those who seek to gain such high profits will, if convicted, be assured that the Canadian people, as represented by parliament, will also extract a high price by way of a minimum penalty of imprisonment without parole. I strongly recommend that, in order to deter this criminal activity and to protect society against this most reprehensible crime, the government should amend the Narcotic Control Act to provide a minimum term of imprisonment of seven years without parole for anyone convicted of trafficking in heroin or possession for the purpose of trafficking in the amount I have mentioned. It may be that parliament, upon examination of my proposal, would see fit to define a commercial trafficker as one who would traffic in, for example, two ounces of heroin which now has a current street value of $25,000. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that one ounce of heroin has a street value of $12,500 while the current value of one ounce of gold is $160.
On September 1, 1973, new drug measures went into effect in the state of New York, just 60 miles from our seat of parliament. There, for example, a person trafficking in one ounce or more of heroin is liable to be sentenced to a minimum term of imprisonment of 15 years, with a maximum of life. While a minimum term of imprisonment is

The Address-Mr. Poulin
repugnant to me generally, and there are very few such penalties remaining in our system of criminal justice, commercial trafficking in heroin is such a heinous crime that I feel it is the duty of parliament to take all the steps it can to deter commercial traffickers and thereby protect society. Those persons who would dare traffic could not do so while in prison.
Commercial trafficking in heroin might better be compared to those criminals responsible for the Lode airport massacre in Israel, the Munich massacre at the 1972 Olympic games or, indeed, if sabotage was involved, the tragic deaths of 344 people in the recent Paris air crash than to a single murder or multiple murder committed in the course of a robbery or a murder committed by an individual under any imaginable circumstances, for the trafficker in heroin leaves his many victims as unfortunate pitiful slaves to a habit that destroys them mentally, morally and physically.
I will quote now from a transcript of the evidence given at a trial by an eminent pharmacologist who holds a Ph.D. and many other high degrees. In addition, at the time of giving this evidence he had 12 years of practical experience in the drug field. His comments on the long-term and immediate effects on an individual of the use of heroin are as follows:
So far as immediate effects in terms of depression of respiration, and depression of heart action; constriction of the pupil of the eye; depression of intestinal movement. Those effects are less apparent in some ways than the behavioural effects, which relate to a lassitude, a languor, almost a stupor; a feeling of well-being, a feeling of comfort and loss of anxiety. That pleasurable feeling is, in fact, one of the reasons that the heroin user returns to the use of the drug.
In the long range, there are additional kinds of effects because heroin use is characterized by two phenomena; the development of tolerance and the development of dependence. The tolerance means that the user has to increase the dose to get the same kind of effect. So that an habitual heroin user will take many time the dose of heroin which would be toxic or perhaps fatal to someone who was not used to taking it. The dependence on the drug is of two kinds: one is a profound craving for the drug, a psychological dependence, which comes to the point of actually mastering the total lifestyle of the user, such that he lives for the drug-taking experience. His whole life experience revolves around the drug-taking and all that he does centres upon an attempt to make certain that he always has the drug in his presence or available to him for his use.
There is, however, a physical dependence which develops for the drug as well. That we know because if you take heroin away from an addict, within a few hours' time he will begin to show the symptoms of withdrawal. In effect, his body cries out against the removal of it-the drug. The withdrawal symptoms include such things as an appearance, almost, of a heavy cold, with running eyes, running nose, the person aches all over; his joints ache, his belly aches; he has stomach cramps, intestinal cramps and sometimes he has unavoidable defecation; he feels absolutely miserable. This lasts for a couple of days in its most acute form. By seven or eight days it is nearly over with, but during that time he feels acutely uncomfortable. Most people who have been involved with heroin and when the drug is taken away, they all go through this withdrawal, but most of them, if left to their own devices, so profound is their psychological dependence on the drug that they will go back and seek the drug again. So the recidivist rate, the percentage of people who voluntarily go back to the use of heroin, when they have been taken off the drug is, even in the best of treatment institutions, 70 or 80 per cent.
All in all the life expectancy of a heroin user is considerably less than that of normal people.
With respect to the usefulness of a heroin user to himself or to society and the possibility of his returning to a

productive life in society, the following evidence was given by the same man:
There is no doubt that the social productivity of heroin users is markedly decreased. Their total lifestyle revolves around the drug. When they are on the drug, they do not want to work; they have a lassitude and a languor about them, almost a stupor; they are not really interested in productive employment; they become a great strain on themselves and their family and society. The number who are able to break away from that is relatively small, even under the best treatment or circumstances most return voluntarily to that kind of a lifestyle.
I have here some interesting statistics involving heroin and its abuse in Canada. In 1969 there were a total of 310 convictions in Canada involving all offences with respect to heroin. In 1972 there were 923 convictions registered with respect to heroin offences in Canada. This is a most alarming comparison. Another most significant statistics with respect to heroin is that in the entire year of 1972 there were 52.94 kilograms-116.56 pounds-seized, whereas in the first nine months of 1973, that is, from January 1, 1973 to September 30, 1973, there were 63.72 kilograms- 140.18 pounds. That is an increase of approximately 20 per cent in the first nine months of 1973 over the amount seized in the previous 12 months. Comparing the same period, the number of persons charged with trafficking in heroin in the entire year 1972 was 958, whereas in the first nine months of 1973 the total number of persons charged with trafficking in heroin was 645.
As I stated earlier, the number of people addicted to this drug has been estimated to be between 16,000 and 19,000. The number of convictions for offences involving heroin shows a tremendous increase between the years 1969- 310-and the year 1972-923. The amount of this illicit substance seized, comparing 1972 and 1973, shows a remarkable increase and the number of individuals charged with trafficking has also been on the increase.
By virtue of the present penalty provision of the Narcotic Control Act a person convicted of trafficking in a narcotic, whether it be cannabis or heroin, is subject to the same penalty, that is, a maximum of life imprisonment. There is, however, no minimum penalty provided presently in the Narcotic Control Act, whether the offence be in relation to trafficking in cannabis or to trafficking in heroin. The minimum penalty in either case, for either substance, is a suspended sentence.
I have the greatest respect for the judges in our country who have in most instances been imposing severe sentences, justifiably so, in the case of those who are found guilty of trafficking in heroin. My recommendation for a minimum sentence of seven years for anyone trafficking commercially in heroin is designed not to take from the judge that discretion, although it would have the effect of doing so, but more to impress upon those who would dare to traffic in this substance the determination of this government and this Parliament to deal with them in the most severe manner in order to deter this trafficking and to protect society. I would also propose, if a person is convicted, for example, of trafficking in four ounces of heroin as I mentioned previously, that the judge, having regard to all the circumstances including the previous criminal record of the person convicted, if any, continue to have the discretion to sentence the person to life imprison-
March 7, 1974

ment. The greatest weapon we have to interrupt and suppress the illicit traffic in this most reprehensible drug is the diligence and honesty of domestic law enforcement, coupled with the most severe penalty for those who would trade in human life in this way for the sole motive of greed, profit and avarice.
A little more than a year ago, Mr. Speaker, we had a throne speech that marked the beginning of some 50 pieces of legislation. This is to be noted because all the pundits at that time were predicting that the government would last for only a matter of weeks, if not days. That session ended, having lasted 203 sitting days. Last week we had another throne speech. In the coming months we will be able to look back on this debate as the beginning of more progressive legislation as long as the majority of members continue to support good Liberal policies such as we have seen defined in the recent throne speech.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member who just sat down because for the last two or three years I have been asking the government of Canada to appoint a royal commission to look into international crime, which includes to a large extent the importation into Canada of those dangerous drugs to which the hon. member referred. I hope that he will now become an ally. Up to now the government has paid little attention to a problem that is serious beyond words. At the same time, I want to say a word about the CBC commentator, Mrs. Trudel, who has dealt with this matter at length on her program. On one occasion last fall I heard her mention how widespread and open trafficking was in this immediate area. Apparently, as a consequence of what she said, the RCMP within the last two weeks picked up a large number of alleged wrongdoers.
At a time like this it is always difficult for one to find subjects on which to speak. The House is waiting for the final vote which will come at the end of this debate but which is of little consequence because, once the amendment of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition-not the official opposition but the opposition-has been turned down, we pass into an area of little or no interest.
I commend the government for its decision to endeavour to make Parliament more effective and representation more equal, for bringing about changes in redistribution so as to assure that large areas of our country with small populations will continue to enjoy a reasonable representation in the House of Commons. I brought this matter up originally, and all parts of the House responded with that degree of desirable co-operation which I have always found to be worthy of notice.
That brings me to this point, Mr. Speaker. Parliament, as operated today under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), is not effective. It is a caricature of what it ought to be. The opposition should place before the people of Canada this fact: we will reform Parliament. We did that in 1956 and 1957. We brought about changes and the people of Canada understood what was happening, because before then the previous administration had been totally disregardful of any views expressed by members in other parts of the House.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
Today two members, by way of privilege, raised the issue of questions asked in the House. 1 have been here for some time. You, Sir, are simply tied up by the rules, many of which were forced through under closure by the majority sitting opposite.

One dare not challenge anything ministers say when they give their truncated answers because, as several hon. members have mentioned, by doing so one would introduce controversial matters. How do you answer controversial matters which may have arisen in a minister's statement except by following up with a supplementary question which may be controversial? What I am leading to is this: There must be a reform of our rules which, today, have placed Parliament in the position of being an adjunct, a necessary adjunct.
As for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the hon. member noted in the House of Commons for his wisdom and warmhearted personality, I have noticed lately that even his warmhearted personality has shown some signs of flagging. He is not in the position of being able to move amendments any more. He cannot do it. He is the authority in the NDP on amendments and on Parliament, but he dare not do anything. Why? Because, if he moved an amendment with the accustomed wisdom that he used in the past, the government would be defeated. It is difficult to express how much Parliament has lost in consequence of the present situation.
Does this House, as presently constituted, discharge its responsibilities? Have we any examination today of expenditures? There is virtually no examination. The No. 1 responsibility of Parliament is to look after supply. What has happened? I knew, when I was Prime Minister that ministers would be concerned about the fact that certain programs would be brought up in the House. You will always have that concern on the part of ministers. Today, you cannot bring those matters up, no matter how wasteful the expenditure or how unjust and improper. There can be no vote in the House of Commons on such items. Two years ago we were placed in the position of having to vote expenditures of $19 billion between eight o'clock and one a.m. Those were fabulous expenditures. Do you mean to tell me that if we could deal with individual items the spendthrift proclivities of the Prime Minister would not receive attention?
If anybody wants any information on the subject of those expenditures, I will render the fullest answer. Not even King Farouk expended to the extent the Prime Minister is doing today on 24 Sussex Drive, his offices and his country place at Harrington Lake. Waste, waste, in the hundreds of thousands of dollars! What can you do? You complain, but nothing happens. Amazing waste! Amazing spendthrift expenditures are being made. They have been revealed by two hon. members, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) and the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt), but you might just as well spit at the moon to do anything effective regarding those expenditures. We have the highest taxation in Canada's history, the highest interest rates-

It is important to commend those whose performance has been responsible and restrained.
The opposition was not included in that.
It is therefore appropriate at this time to destroy the myth that the cost of labour has been a dominant factor contributing to the present inflationary round in Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture has not expressed a similar view, but this is the official view now. Having slapped labour in the face for four years, the Prime Minister has suddenly decided that the responsibility for inflation is not theirs. He went on to say that it was not true that the average working man has caused excessive upward pressure on prices.
One of these days I am going to make a speech about all the criticism that was heaped on my head at one time, because some of the members opposite seem to have forgotten that we were in office. They seem to have forgotten the fact that in the period to which I am referring we enjoyed the lowest rate of inflation of any country in the world. How was it done? Simply by having a vociferous minister like the Minister of Transport. If word came that there were to be increases which we believed to be unjustified, the heads of those corporations were contacted and asked whether it was true. We inquired why, and very often they said it was because of increased costs. You would be amazed, Mr. Speaker, how quickly these plutocrats said, "We have not decided on the matter yet", when it was pointed out that if they did, an examination would be made under the Combines Investigation Act and if the increases were not justified they would be prosecuted. Today there is open season on the manner in which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) and the other ministers, including the Prime Minister, look after inflation. It goes up, up, up.
The day before yesterday they saw the light. They followed the course followed by certain of my ministers and got in touch with the bread people. Yesterday the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was able to say that there would not be an increase to the four cents. Westons agreed to this the day before yesterday. Then the minister came out with the No. 1 government policy of all and told Canadians that if they did not cut down, boycott them, ignore them. There is the government's policy.

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
Mention has been made of the actual rate of inflation. Mr. St. Laurent was not a spendthrift. He did not waste the people's money or live in glorified greatness. Under his government the rate of inflation was 2.04 per cent. Under the government of Mr. Pearson the rate was 3.26 per cent. He never indulged in self-glorification. He lived in the home I lived in when I was Prime Minister and was most economical in office. Under my administration the rate of inflation was 1.4 per cent.
What is the rate today, Mr. Speaker? The average of this government has been at least 6.7 per cent. The government has done nothing but spend, spend, waste and tax, and then they wonder why the people are asking what can be done to control inflation. Everyone rushes to spend their money as fast as they get it so it does not lose its value.
Going back to 1971, after the Prime Minister announced that we had inflation beaten the rate stood at 1.6 per cent and by the end of the year had risen to 5 per cent. By the end of 1972 it was up to 5.1 per cent, in 1973 up to 9.1 per cent, and the rate today is 9.1 per cent. When is the government going to decide that the people's money should not be wasted? That is the simple question. But the government will not answer it because everyone is engaged in spending and nobody cares. There is no control.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will restrict my remarks to the next five minutes before adjournment.
What are the government's policies in the field of agriculture? Reporting for the Wheat Board, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) has said that all is well. The government brought in the LIFT program. When I returned from the Far East and the U.S.S.R. I said that the demand for wheat was going to be beyond anything we had had before. At that very time the government of Canada called on the western farmers to cut down production. I opposed the LIFT program in the light of events, and I am able to say now that by following the LIFT policy of the government of Canada the western farmer lost hundreds of millions of dollars.
Why cannot some action be taken with respect to boxcars? This morning I decided to turn to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), and I hope he does not turn away from what he said. We have been trying for months to get the Minister of Justice to bring in legislation to provide that these great railway companies shall not defy the people. Each area of the economy ought to receive its fair share. I suggested a controller with the power to direct that a fair share of available cars be given to grain movement. This is not the case today. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) pointed out that cars were piled up for weeks, unused. In explanation all we got was a snow job from the government. The minister says that when the snow goes, everything will be well. Why will this government not appoint a controller?

I am glad to see that at last the Liberal party has awakened to the need for an international food bank. They speak of it today as if it were a recent discovery, a product of the mind of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). I never charge him with coming to conclusions on anything and I know there is no basis for that.
I brought this question up in December, 1957, before the NATO conference in the city of Paris. All the leaders were there for the first and last time. Only two nations joined, Canada and Norway, no one else. Then, in September of 1960 before the United Nations I brought up the suggestion of a world food bank, but again there were difficulties. However, today other nations are beginning to learn, and Canada is beginning to learn.
I had hoped to deal with international affairs, Mr. Speaker, because, if ever there was a mess in Canada, the administration of international affairs today is in a class by itself. Finally, I ask when will the government give the western wheat farmer immediate interim payments to the end that he does not have to continue to pay interest at a rate of 9, 10 or 12 per cent?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would probably have been unforgivable, on the occasion of the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne and after one year at the head of the Department of Transport, if I had not found the time despite the circumstances to tell the House about the situation as concerns the Department of Transport and about the future as I see it.

I want this speech to be as non-political as possible. I do not know how successful I will be, but I will judge from your reaction. In any event, I tell you that is what I am going to try to do as I think this is a problem so important to the future of this country that we should, at least for a few hours, look into each other's eyes and say what we really think about this matter.
Before preparing my notes for this speech I looked through Hansard for the past 20 years in an attempt to find a comprehensive speech on transportation as a whole, not just on one aspect or a philosophy of the moment. Unfortunately, I did not find such a speech. I found speeches delivered by a number of persons which were good in respect of a particular purpose, but I did not find a speech which covered npt only the problems of the moment but the problems to be encountered in the future.
The last great speeches on transportation were made back in 1967 when the National Transportation Act was adopted by the House. At that time we, as a government, laid down a number of principles in which we believed.
March 7, 1974

These principles were not really rejected by the opposition. Of course, there was opposition but not in respect of the main principles. We said at that time that transportation should work in the same way as other things in other sectors of the economy. We suggested that we should have competition between the railway companies as well as competition between the railways and the trucking industry and between the trucking industry and the shipping industry. We felt in that way we would be sure of getting the best deal possible in this field. I was here at that time and I do not remember hearing any indication of any reservation about this principle. I can tell you now in all honesty from my experience that this fundamental principle is wrong in Canada. It is not entirely wrong but is partially wrong, because if you look at the size of this country and the distribution of its population you will see that you cannot have a transportation network which is economic everywhere; you cannot have an economic system of transportation to service the north, for example, or to service those regions of the country where the population is very thin. You cannot have an economic system for regions which are remote from the centre.
Let us speak about the Maritimes, for instance. If we had laid down this principle at the same time or immediately after we had passed those laws which enable either the department or the CTC to subsidize a certain part of the country, not only the Maritimes but other regions would have suffered. That means that the fundamental principle can apply where there is competition in Canada at this moment, but it will not work in the many places in which there is no competition.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was not true in 1967.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I believe we thought this experiment would bring results in all regions but this has not happened. I am sure the CNR does not have competition in certain regions. The same applies to the CPR. Sometimes they agree not to have any competition. The fundamental principle of this act has been distorted by the situation in Canada. This is the reason there are so many complaints. I shall not attempt to say to this House that everything that has been done since I have been in office has been perfect. I shall not attempt to prove that.

speechtext: We agree.

You agree. I am glad to hear that you agree with something. Sometimes I am pushed around a little in the House by some tricky questions because in the transportation field there can be a lot of difficult situations. I believe I can say I have been lucky. In any event, I think it is correct to say that many good things have been accomplished during this past year and a half I have been in this ministry. I do not say this for myself but on behalf of all the public servants who work hard to solve certain problems, as they did in respect of the problem of the freight rates in the Maritimes. There was an increase from 30 per cent to 50 per cent in the subsidy on westbound traffic. They were successful in working out that formula. I believe everything is just
The Address-Mr. J. Marchand about settled now and we will have an agreement on this question very soon.
So, that has been done and it is very important. That does not mean we have solved all the problems of the Maritimes, but it is something we can place on the right side or on the left side of the ledger. I am not an accountant, so I do not know which side is the good side.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The right side.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Then, let us put it on the right side. We dealt with the famous Darling report. For years this problem was never solved, but now it has been solved. We have agreed on a formula which will provide that coastal shipping in Canada will be carried on only by Canadian ships and Canadian crews when they are available. So, if we add that to the restrictions we are placing on shipping in Arctic waters, this means that sooner or later we will have something that will look like a merchant marine in Canada. There are many other reasons to believe this is the direction toward which we are moving. This is something positive which is worthwhile mentioning.
We speak also a great deal today about the Western Economic Opportunities Conference and its effects on the western provinces. I have heard statements to the effect that nothing has happened since the meeting in Calgary six or seven months ago. Well, this is not true. I have met twice with the ministers of transport and I shall meet with them again in Vancouver sometime next week. All these ministers agree that if we are to change the pricing systems of the railways in respect of freight, this cannot be done overnight. A proposal was made by Manitoba and another was made by Alberta. We agreed to have a firm of specialists study these and make recommendations. We all agreed that this study could not be available before the month of May or June. The fact there has been no result yet is because we agreed that there should be this kind of consultation. Now, we hope to have some kind of an answer. We agreed on that.
We are agreeing now on the upgrading of the highways on the Prairies. We agreed to freeze all branch lines. This has been done. I hope we still have agreement with the province of British Columbia concerning the rail and port development in the north of the province. This involves an amount of $325 million for the development not only of the natural resources of the north but also the port of Prince Rupert. This is something which is there; no one can deny it. There is also the matter of the Clinton-Ashcroft bypass on which we have a clear agreement. Everyone agrees this is good.
A large amount of money is being spent in Calgary for the new airport. This is something new and it is on the right side of the ledger. We have a new international air policy for the international carriers, CP Air and Air Canada. This is new. It is not perfect. However, I know this has really helped both air lines. It will help not only in solving disputes between CP Air and Air Canada but also with the main problem of getting the largest share we can of the international market. This is what we have done. This is a fact. It is something positive. So, we have signed a bilateral air agreement with the United States. Some people may say it is rotten and they do not like it in

respect of their areas, but others say it is good. I shall not discuss its merits, but I know it is the largest bilateral agreement ever signed in the world. This opens many markets. I believe in the long run after we open United States markets to Canadians we will win because it is a larger market and we have a good chance of having a better return. This is something else that should be placed on the right side of the ledger.
In the matter of airports, we thought we could build an airport at Pickering to service Toronto. I am not responsible for that, and if it is proven that it is useless to have an airport there then I am not going to insist on the expenditure of $400 million.

To be sure of not losing my mother tongue, I would try to explain a few things as briefly as possible in French. Are we really going to stay indefinitely in this closed circle, which is the essence of a circle, or are we going to broaden somewhat our transportation policy and see how we will serve the Canadian people in the future? That is the important thing. Then it is not simply... and by way of an answer I could very well say that we will try to build more railroad cars to carry lumber, coal, or western wheat. It can and will probably be done, but the transportation policy has not been basically changed.

The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) was telling me this morning of the wheat problem in the west. He is right. Railway companies are indeed not interested in carrying wheat. It is not profitable; they have been shaken by the present situation and do not want to buy cars to carry wheat. Even is they were paid, I doubt that they would do it. So there is quite a problem. Government cannot discuss indefinitely. The external trade of the country greatly needs an effective transportation system, giving a fast and safe service, for Canada is an exporting country. Actually, the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific companies do not have available for Canadians more cars than they had last year.

About the same number of box cars are available this year as we had last year. This means that no provision was made for any growth in the economy. This is true. So, what do we do in this situation? Hon. members may say, "You are the minister; you do it." I have a few answers to that, Mr. Speaker. It is true that hon. members gave responsibilities to the minister, but they forgot to give any authority at all in many instances.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I am just talking to the House. I told you I would not make a political speech. I am just trying to tell you the facts. Everything is done the same way. We have the CTC which has final authority over almost everything, except in a few cases where there is provision for an appeal to the minister.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that we decided to have two national carriers. You know in this country we like to have everything in duplicate-two languages, two great ethnic groups, two railways, two national flag air carriers. We like to have two of everything. We do not like to be alone.

Mr. Speaker, you can understand that in such a short time I will not have the opportunity to go over all the problems, but the problem of the freight cars is a real one. We were fortunate that we did buy a certain number of hopper cars last year. As a result the railways own a number of cars, and the Wheat Board owns a certain number of cars. I do not know if there is a possibility we may buy some more as a result of other governmental re-organization.
Then, there is the question of regional air carriers. Very often I hear hon. members make speeches on the philosophy that should govern our aviation policies. Air Canada is a national carrier. Then, we decided to have another one. But often hon. members will say, "That is fine, but what are you doing for my locality? It is more important." At present we have PWA, Quebecair, Nordair, Wardair, EPA in the west, and Transair. I apologize for mentioning Wardair because it is not a regional carrier.
March 7, 1974

When an airline is designated a regional carrier it often enters the charter business in order to maintain a satisfactory economic condition. Then, it will turn around and tell us, "We have to stay in the charter business to remain economic, and we will have to abandon some local or regional routes." What do we do in that situation? Are we to establish a third carrier system? That would be silly. The third carrier would also buy big jets in a few years, and in order to pay for them it would need routes that extended beyond the particular locality or region originally awarded to it. That might make sense, as a result of which at that stage we will have big regional carriers with big jets, a third system of carriers with big jets, and we will be on our way to creating a fourth system of carriers. This is precisely the policy that was followed in the United States, with the direct result that many companies went bankrupt.
We also have the problem of isolation in Canada. There are communities far away from the bulk of the population. They need a service, and in return we say, "If you can find an airline which is going to make money servicing your area, then all right we will build you an airport." That means we will have Canadians who will not be serviced and who will remain isolated from the rest of the country. You can say, well, this is public money and we should use public money in order that those people will feel they are Canadians, so we have to give them service.
Then, there are all the problems of urban transportation and these are very serious ones. I remember about six months ago when I flew to Paris the journey took five hours, 45 minutes but from Orly airport into Paris took one hour and 45 minutes.

But I do not want to talk about the past, Mr. Speaker. We do not have what we can call a real policy for the future. If I stay in this post I shall surely ask the authority of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet to try to elaborate this kind of policy so that we know where we are going.
This morning we were talking of snow in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Of course, this is not new; snow in Canada is a very old feature of our country. Maybe we will have to stockpile some rolling stock somewhere. Do we always have to establish a level of rolling stock, for example, exactly at the level of economic activity in Canada or should we be wiser and say that even if it costs money it is better to build more freight cars and have them in reserve? This would meet a situation such as the one we encountered this winter in which there was a shortage of rail cars for lumber, a shortage of cars for wheat, for fruits and almost everything, even for moving grain to the east. At the same time we had too many cars in the maritimes; some were waiting in Sydney to be crossed over to Newfoundland. I am not going to tell you that I am building rail cars in my yard, because I am not. I am sure of one thing, however; I do not think we can go very far in this country without a policy in that field which is much more far-reaching then the one we have followed nationally until now. Everybody tried to contribute suggestions because this is a problem which is vital to the country.
As minister, you will understand that I am responsible for the ministry of transport. I would like hon. members to visit the ministry so that they could find out exactly what it is. There are three large sections of this administrations-air, marine and surface. As well as that there are many Crown corporations such as the National Harbours Board, the seaway, four pilotage authorities, CNR, Air Canada, Northern Transportation and so on and so forth. Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to follow an orator of the stature of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). At the risk of having hon. members thumping their desks again may I say, through you, that it was a fine speech and I enjoyed it. It is a tough act to follow.
It is with some regret that I enter this throne speech debate today, Mr. Speaker. On January 16, last year, very shortly after the opening of the first session of this parliament I spoke at some length about some very serious concerns with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Those concerns are as great today, indeed, even greater, and I intend to dwell for a few moments solely on this very unhappy situation.

Before I do, however, let me say that as I read over the comments I made at that time I recall congratulating you, Mr. Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker, on your elections to the onerous duties of your offices. After this past year I feel I am now in a position to pass judgment on the handling of these offices with at least some small experience. I can only say now that my remarks at that time were traditional and frankly not sufficiently commendatory. I am extremely impressed with the manner in which Your Honour handles the daily challenge of this House with firmness and yet complete grace, especially during times when members both new and old, myself included, must strain the patience of Your Honour to the breaking point. I thank you for the many courtesies afforded to me. These same comments, in a like degree, must also be accorded to the Deputy Speaker, who has brought to his position a calm patience which, I understand, was not his trademark prior to his election to this office. His grasp of the intricacies of the task has been exceptional.
I also want to say a word of appreciation to the two assistant acting speakers for their efficiency and fairness, as shown to me when I have risen to speak. If I may reflect for one further moment, you will recall that I spoke, as is customary, of the many great qualities of the riding of Hastings, which I am proud to represent. If there is a member in this House now who is not aware of the qualities of that riding or even of the excellent cheese which we produce, I will have erred grievously and I shall correct that error as soon as possible.
Now, let me speak of my major concern, that of the tragedy of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In reviewing my remarks of the year past I noted that I brought to Your Honour's attention, and to the attention of those in a position to make corrections, a number of details which I felt surely would have warranted a serious study. During the intervening space of over 13 months I have repeatedly brought to the attention of the minister, other members of the cabinet and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), both in this House and in statements outside the House, a need for a full-fledged inquiry, this being the only way that we can properly expect to achieve any semblance of order out of this very disordered piece of legislation.
I suppose it might give a minister of the Crown some small pleasure when he thwarts a member of the opposition in his attempt to achieve a specific correction in that minister's field; but when hundreds of thousands of Canadians do not receive proper treatment at the hands of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, when many Canadians, through no fault of their own, need assistance, and, what is even more important in my mind, when the many millions of Canadians who have to pay the exorbitant rates charged by the Unemployment Insurance Commission have little or no hope of collecting benefits and see no end to this most disgusting form of indirect taxation, then, when these many Canadians become as unhappy as I am, I think the minister may well have thwarted a section of the Canadian public, to his everlasting discomfort.
It is interesting to note that I started to demand an inquiry into this matter on January 16, 1973; and mine was
March 7, 1974

a lone voice at that time. Since then, the Canadian Construction Association, the Retail Merchants Association of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the Chamber of Commerce and many other associations representing Canadians from all walks of life, have joined in my request for such an inquiry. While I have had support from members of my party throughout all this, I am very pleased and proud that just recently the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) formally, on behalf of the party, issued a similar request to the minister for a full-fledged inquiry. As a matter of fact I had hoped, from the report of a press conference by the minister after a speech at the Canadian Construction Association in Quebec, that there would indeed be consideration of an inquiry. At that time I suggested publicly to the minister that he might well ask that some indication of this be included in the Speech from the Throne which we are discussing now. Unfortunately, the following day, in Cobalt, the minister denied ever making such a statement.
I know that the press have a tendency sometimes to shade or colour or slightly change what we, as practising politicians, from time to time say; but, Mr. Speaker, they do not make up such statements out of whole cloth. No, indeed! I suspect very strongly that in the presence of some of the heavyweights of the Canadian Construction Association the minister began to realize the enormity of the request and the need for such an inquiry all across Canada. Who got to the minister after that to have him reverse himself at a time and place when there would be no pressure I do not know. Suffice it to say I am deeply disappointed and curious as to what he is trying to hide.
Let me explore for a moment the need for an inquiry. In a document which I prepared some months ago and which is available to any who asks, I contended that almost $1 billion had been distributed throughout the Unemployment Insurance Commission to people who were not deserving of assistance. That, Mr. Speaker, is a particularly strong statement, one which I researched very, very thoroughly before making. While there have been, from time to time, scandals within governments at all levels in this country and in other countries, I doubt if there has ever been such a wastage of funds collected from taxpayers in modern times. Very briefly, so that there will be no question in anyone's mind, I ask people only to take the figures given by the minister as to the number of disqualifications made in the latter part of 1973. Assuming that the level of disqualifications would have been as great from the inception of the new legislation, and multiplying that by the average amount of a claim, you will come to a figure of well over $850 million. My contention that almost $1 billion has been improperly distributed is very easily substantiated.
In my opinion it does no good for the previous minister to say that this money was a new kind of social distribution of wealth, that it, in fact, actually helped the economy. If we are to have welfare programs, let's do them honestly; let's do them humanely; let's do them only where necessary, but let's not call them an Unemployment Insurance program. There were, and are, many other accusations in the document I referred to and I have added to the list since. It is interesting to have the minister, in his recent speech, admit that the charges which had been
The Address-Mr. Ellis
made, and I assume he refers to my charges, were accurate.
At one point in my discussion of these problems I pointed out that in my opinion the level of collections would be completely insufficient to balance the fund. Despite denials late last year, there was a major increase in premiums, ostensibly a 40 per cent increase but in actual fact an increase ranging as high as 98 per cent, to some Canadians.
I suggest to the minister that the increases which he implemented, unless there are major changes in the legislation and unless some of the abuses are curtailed, will not come anywhere close to balancing the books this year, next year or in the years to come. Employers and employees alike have threatened they will not pay the increased premiums.
Let me just point this out as a means of comparison. The budget for administration for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, which supposedly only services approximately 6 per cent of the working population who are unemployed, cost taxpayers $145 million in 1973. By contrast, the administration of the Income Tax Division of the Department of National Revenue, which collects from every Canadian, employed, unemployed, or retired on a continuing basis every day of every week of every year, in 1973 cost taxpayers only $136 million. I am unaware of the relative efficiency of the Income Tax Division. Perhaps there is some fat there also; but, surely in a comparison of the two figures one can only shudder at the obvious inefficiency of the UIC.
Another salient comparison, particularly since the government blames its problems on outside influence, can be made if one looks at the unemployment situation in the United States. There, the level of unemployment is within one half per cent of ours, but wages run about 20 per cent higher. The unemployment insurance figures suffer terribly by comparison. The average Canadian recipient of UIC assistance received $2,328 last year, while the average U.S. recipient received $768. In the United States, the cost of unemployment insurance equalled 2 per cent of the budget. In Canada it was 10 per cent. Although Canada's population is only 10 per cent of the United States, the cost of the unemployment insurance in Canada is 50 per cent of the U.S.; our cost of $2.1 billion versus theirs of $4.1 billion. In 1970, our programs on a pro rated basis were about equal. How many more comparisons are needed to prompt an honest inquiry?
Let me for a minute make a few interesting points to those hon. members sitting on my far left; far left, supposedly, in more ways than one. The NDP supposedly is the party of the labour unions. The NDP admits, and yes, even brags that they were successful in keeping Bill C-125 from becoming legislation during the first session of this parliament. Not that perhaps Bill C-125 was a perfect answer by any manner or means. Indeed, in my opinion, it was similar to the ad hocery that has taken place, but let us consider the way the members of this party represent their unions. I suggest that the average union employee is ripped off by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, harder by far, in fact four times over, than any other average Canadian. Let me explain.

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Ellis
The union employee is the one who is the least likely to be laid off. He is the one who bargains in his contract, and rightly so, for security. It is the many thousands of unorganized workers in Canada who normally make up the larger share of those receiving unemployment insurance benefits. The union employee, if he has any program for providing him with assistance from his regular employer for any layoff, gets no help from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, or at least very little. Thus it is that the average union employee is less in need of this program than any other. However, it is the union employee who pays the largest share of the premiums. The average union employee who makes over $170 weekly, enough to put him in the category of paying the maximum premiums, is the type of employee whose rates were increased by 48.7 per cent in January of this year. It is this type of employee, if he happens to be in one of those areas which were added to the work force at the inception of this legislation, whose premiums were increased by 98 per cent. Therefore, the average union employee pays more in direct premiums.
In addition, the average union employee provides a great deal of the purchasing power in Canada. The employer, the manufacturer, the producer who is being charged 1.96 per cent of wages does not actually pay those amounts himself. Rather, he adds that amount directly to the cost of the goods and services he provides and, once again, it is the average union employee who picks up the tab by purchasing those goods and services. There is no way he can prevent this situation.
Finally, the fund is not, by the wildest stretch of the imagination, self-sustaining and a good deal of the money being disbursed comes from the general rate. It is the average union employee who, through direct income taxation, pays a major portion of the income taxes which go to make up those many billions of dollars that are being distributed through this fund. In my constituency, a number of union employees are very unhappy with the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Much has been made of the documents which I have in my possession. The most ludicrous outcome of this situation was the instigation of an investigation by the RCMP as to the source of those documents. I have far too much respect for the RCMP, probably one of the finest police forces in the whole world, to ever believe that they would have started such a ridiculous and asinine project of their own volition. No, they had to be directed to do so, and I suggest that direction had to come from the minister of the Crown responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission. If that minister was not responsible for instigating that investigation, then I suggest to him that he find out who was responsible.
It was obvious after my discussion with the officers involved that they had been badly misled because they fully anticipated that the documents I had in my possession would be marked "confidential". This of course, is not the case. I do not like the sensationalism caused by using documents in this nature. Had there been anything, in any minute way a threat to security, I swear I would not have used it.
There is, however, a document which I have not referred to yet and, before I go any further, let me state categorically it is not marked "confidential". To the best of my

knowledge, it is the only remaining one of its kind since the chairman of the commission was very careful to have the remainder of them destroyed. It did not come to me from a civil servant working within or without the Unemployment Insurance Commission so there is no question of breach of oath. I have, however, carefully checked its authenticity and am thoroughly convinced of its validity.
I have now to turn my attention to the former minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), since I cannot by any stretch of the imagination centre my criticism of the formation of the legislation on the present minister. I am now in a position to state categorically that in February of 1970, months before the legislation came into effect, the knowledge was available that a mistake, a gross error, had been made in the calculations used to estimate the cost of the disability program that was to be implemented. This error, in the range of $200 million to $300 million was known. I ask if the hon. member for Verdun was aware that that error had been made, discovered and was not being corrected. Through the many months of interrogation and investigation before the standing committee, my colleagues who were in the House at that time constantly questioned the validity of these figures, since to many it was obvious there had to be an error.
There was an error and someone responsible knew there was an error. I ask the hon. member for Verdun, did he know that such an error was being perpetrated in the presentation of the statistics that were used in the preparation of this legislation? If he did know, then with a great deal of reluctance I state that he was dishonest in not bringing it to the attention of the committee. If he did not know of this error and since we have debated the matter publicly on many occasions-I admire the hon. member for Verdun personally and I would much prefer to think that he did not know-I suggest to him he has no recourse but to join with me in my request for an inquiry into this matter alone, if nothing else.
The approach of the present minister to my many allegations has been, unfortunately, typical. At one point when I questioned him with regard to the increase of computer facilities at the regional pay centre, in Belleville, he indicated that there were no enlargements planned. Those enlargements are in place and functioning at almost double the original capacity. On another occasion when questioned about the computers, the minister blamed staff. At that time I took very strong exception, and I continue to take strong exception to that approach. My investigation, and indeed the investigation undertaken by the Department of Supply and Services not that long ago in the province of Quebec, resulted in a clear indication that the average employee of the commission is, by and large, a hard-working civil servant. In the words of the department itself, had it not been for the dedication of these people, the commission could not have weathered the extremely difficult conditions during the early years of the legislation.
The approach has been to install new locks, to change the keys of the existing locks and in the case of the Belleville Regional Pay Centre, to put on a massive lock costing over $600 which prevents anyone on staff from
March 7, 1974

entering the executive suite. The cost of the lock and the cost of installing the lock are outrageous. It is the typical approach of the minister and his department that they would take Gestapo-like methods in an effort to prevent the Canadian public knowing exactly what is going on in the Commission before they make even the feeblest attempt to correct this situation. Again I ask: What are they trying to hide?
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has conducted surveys. I have conducted surveys. Others have conducted surveys. They all underline the need for an inquiry. Virtually every newspaper, radio station and television network in the country has commented on such a need. The major associations which I mentioned earlier have demanded an inquiry. In the name of all that is reasonable, what does a Canadian have to do in order to bring about such an inquiry? The avoidance of an inquiry in order to maintain the ego of the few whose interests are perhaps best served by not digging into the matter thoroughly is a position which will not much longer be accepted by Canadians in any walk of life.
The Speech from the Throne spoke of a comprehensive review. That is just not satisfactory. It is not sufficient. It will not do. The Canadian public will not accept the whitewash job perpetrated upon them by the very people who were the cause of the problem in the first place. It may well afford some satisfaction to the minister to thwart me in my efforts but I suggest to him that should he continue to do so much longer, with the increasing pressure from Canadians in every province, he will do so at very considerable risk. And, I suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) there will be considerable risk to him, also.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate in order to say something about what I regard as being Canada's most pressing national problem to the extent that it affects the greatest number of people directly today. I refer to housing. I listened with a great deal of interest yesterday to the speech given by the Minister of State responsible for housing in the hope of hearing him announce new programs to deal with what might properly be described as a crisis situation in housing. What did I hear? I heard the hon. member from British Columbia speak for ten minutes on harbours, all of which were located, of course, in British Columbia. Then, he spoke for another ten minutes on railways. Again, all
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
the railway development to which he referred happens to be in British Columbia.
Toward the end of his speech he deigned to spend a few minutes on the subject of housing. But nowhere was there any indication that the government intends, at least before the budget is introduced, to move in a serious way to deal with the housing situation. There is every indication that in this area of policy we are saddled with a do-nothing government, a government which, once the housing bill was passed last spring, decided, presumably, that enough had been accomplished.
Let me put forward my reasons for believing that such an attitude is palpably absurd. Indeed, it is more than absurd since it involves a serious question of social morality, and the government has "copped out" altogether on this issue. To put the subject into some kind of perspective, let me compare it with the so-called fuel crisis. What does it mean for Canadians? I do not wish to be misunderstood. In the long run we shall face a fuel crisis in Canada, especially in the years beyond 1980. We shall be confronted with serious shortages and plans must be made now to deal with them. But in the short run, which countries face an oil crisis? Western Europe does, and so does Japan, since the oil used there has to be imported. But a man in Tokyo or a woman reading the headlines of her newspaper in Brussels, could scarcely bring themselves to believe that Canada, a country self-sufficient in oil, was really facing a fuel crisis. In reality, the current "crisis" centres on the amount which one part of Canada will charge another part of Canada for its products. As to the effect of the present situation in terms of cash, a typical family will be paying $50 more for heating their home over the six months winter period. In the same six months, given the present rate of inflation in the housing industry, the price of the home itself will have increased by $4,000. When we make that kind of comparison, it is abundantly clear where the national political energy should be going at this time.
Let me give the House some further information as to what is happening in the housing field. In Ottawa, Toronto and Vancouver, prices have increased in the past year by some 25 per cent. In virtually all of urban Canada the picture is the same. For the first time in Canadian history a steadily-employed, moderate income family living in Canada cannot afford to buy a housing unit, whether a single family dwelling, a condominium, or other kind of accommodation. The reason for this is that governments at the federal level in the past, both Liberal and Conservative, have failed to recognize that housing is to be distinguished from other goods and services available in the commodity market. They have regarded housing as being basically like any other consumer item. They have refrained from interfering with the financial markets or with the acquisition of land because, in their view, a house is like a television set or an electric toothbrush or any other item of consumer use. Price, in their view, must correspond with market conditions.
Thus, the situation which exists today is a very bad one-and I say this with great deliberation-it will become worse in the next three or four years. The generation born in the late 'forties or early 'fifties is now coming into the housing market. A number of crises have already

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
arisen in connection with that generation. First, there was the elementary school crisis; the number of places in elementary schools had to be expanded rapidly to meet the need. This was followed by the need for a similar dramatic expansion of places available in our high schools and, later, in our post-secondary institutions. These same people are now young parents with one or two children; they are out in the housing market in every city from St. John's to Vancouver.
I point out in passing that we are among the most highly urbanized people in the world with almost 85 per cent of our population in the cities-a higher proportion than in the United States. Moreover, the proportion in the age group normally buying houses, the proportion with young families, is the highest in the western industrialized world. This means that a housing crisis of significant proportions is upon us, and it will continue if we allow the normal market situation to continue unchanged. If we want to do that, it means that we have to abandon the typical approach to housing used by both the Liberal and Conservative parties in Canada. What have these parties done? In the past they have relied on profit incentives. In 1967 they combined together to lift the 6 per cent ceiling on bank mortgages.
In 1969 the Liberals and Tories voted in favour of lifting the 6'/2 per cent NHA ceiling on mortgages. In the same year, the former minister responsible for housing in a Liberal government, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who now sits as a Conservative, recommended that we introduce a rollover period on mortgages of five years. The idea was justified politically at that time on the ground that when you take out a mortgage at one point, five years later the interest might come down and the mortgage payments are thus reduced. But what has happened, of course, has been that ever since this feature was introduced in 1969 mortgage rates have not gone down, but both Liberals and Tories were happy to accept the profit incentive idea.
Again, both these parties combined together three months ago in this House to vote for the mortgage mechanisms bill. In the immortal words of the minister responsible for housing, the purpose of this bill was to enhance the attractiveness of investments in mortgages. The cumulative effect of the reliance on the profit motive, clearly argued for by both Liberals and Conservatives, is that during the Trudeau years, when the four innovations I have just mentioned were introduced, average or low income housing disappeared from the housing market and high income houses appeared like they had never appeared before in this country. The profit margins of the financial institutions of Canada went almost out of sight and have been almost at the highest level in Canadian history. Mortgage rates now are around 10 per cent.
The average price of a house for sale in Toronto is $41,000. According to NHA regulations, you would require an income of $21,600 to purchase that home. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how many people in the city of Toronto earn $21,600? Maybe 5 per cent, 10 per cent at the most. The NHA authority, which was set up to enable the average person in Canada living in a city or urban area to finance

the purchase of a home, is now assisting only the top 5 or 10 per cent of the income earners in our population.
This same reliance upon and encouragement of profit incentives has led the banks to invest in mortgages like they have never invested before. I have already referred to the high profit levels of financial institutions. Bank profits in particular have risen 85 per cent during the past five years. These figures are significant and I wish the minister responsible for housing were in the chamber. We will see what is going to happen with his financial mechanisms legislation when it takes effect this year. Last year banks in Canada increased their mortgage investment by 67 per cent; in 1973 their investment was up 67 per cent over 1972. The reason for this is obvious; there is no better place in Canada to make a quick buck, a very substantial return, than to invest in mortgages, which is exactly what the banks are doing.
I could list the profits made by a number of major corporations involved in other aspects of house financing or land development, but I will mention only one, Cadillac Development Corporation. This is not a small concern but one with holdings in Ottawa, Toronto, Mississauga, Windsor, Hamilton, Hull and in the U.S.A. It is a Canadian multinational corporation. If we look at this corporation's profit picture for the nine months ending September 30, 1973 we find profits increased 57.1 per cent over the same period in 1972. Their profits from land and housing increased 214 per cent. This is the profit made by one of our larger development corporations, but is quite typical of Campeau and a dozen other development corporations I could mention. However, I will not bore the House with all the statistics.
Quite apart from the financing of houses, which has become crucial in terms of cost, the other important aspect of housing costs is land. Land costs during the last three years have gone up, on average in Canada, by 60 per cent. Last year the average increase in our largest cities was 20 per cent. I am not at all happy to say that I learned only yesterday that the city I represent, Oshawa, now has the dubious honour of having the highest lot costs in Canada. According to figures not yet released by Statistics Canada but which will be coming out soon, the cost of the average lot in the city of Oshawa is now $14,875. This is on an NHA financed housing project and is the highest average in Canada. The average cost of a housing lot across Canada that is not NHA financed is even higher than this scandalously distressing figure of $14,875. What has brought this about? Again we have left to free market forces the buying and selling of our land. With the increased numbers of persons entering the housing market at this time, what can one expect? One can expect a few people to make a lot of money if the market is left to operate on its own.
Many hon. members are aware that the Globe and Mail published an interesting investigative report last spring. It revealed that of all the land available and designated for housing development in metro Toronto, some 80 per cent was owned by five companies. These companies are now in the market for one reason and for one reason only-to make a speculative land profit. That is where the big gain is to be made in our major urban centres, and it is where they put their money.
March 7, 1974

Let me give an example of the wheeling and dealing of just one company, Consolidated Building Corporation of Toronto. In July of 1973 this fine, noble, altruistic corporation bought 18 acres of land and resold it 17 days later for a profit of $1.5 million. That is not bad for 17 days. This company is in the land development business and has extensive residential and commercial holdings in and around the city of Toronto. However, in 1973 they found that land speculation in itself, not simply land development, was a more attractive business than building homes. According to the president of the company, as quoted in the Globe and Mail, the company is a public company and in the business of making profit. He used that fact to justify the company's total concentration upon land speculation.
