speechtext:
Good capitalist theory, as my colleague says. The people who pay for this kind of theory are the countless thousands who want to buy a home in one of the cities of Canada at the present time.
What can be done to correct the situation, Mr. Speaker? Clearly we have to abandon once and for all the notion that market forces can be left to treat houses in the same way as they treat television sets and similar commodities, which is to let people pay what the market will bear. This kind of thinking must be abandoned. We have to regard housing as we regard the provision of schools and medicare: it belongs by right to all Canadians, not simply to those in fortunate circumstances. What is required to bring this about? It requires direct government involvement, just as did the building of schools for our children during the past century, and just as did the provision of medicare services during the past decade.
Let me suggest two specific courses of action. In order to deal with financing of housing we must say to the banks, the trust companies and the insurance companies that they hold savings of Canadians and can make legitimate profits on most of their investments, but in the area of housing they will have to put up mortgage money at an interest rate which will not produce a profit. We should say that very explicitly. We must say to the banks, by a change to the Bank Act here in the House of Commons, that they must put up mortgage money at 6 per cent, and we must change other financial legislation which applies to other financial insititutions to achieve a similar effect.
I suggest that we should make sure we have a vigorous department of housing rather than be satisfied with the current situation in which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) makes fine, well-intended speeches but does nothing. We should have an active department of housing whose responsibility it would be to allocate that 6 per cent mortgage money to the moderate and low income group first, and then to the upper income group when the needs of the first groups were met. I suggest in all seriousness if this were started now we could provide mortgage money so that 90 per cent of the families in Canada could afford housing without a serious impact on their monthly budgets.
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
The second approach we must take has to do with the land matter. What can be done there? As the minister of state responsible for housing knows, in the 15 larger cities in Canada there are 50,000 acres of what is called quick-start land now available. This is land that can be used for housing almost immediately. If this government wanted to act in this regard, all it would have to do is buy the 50,000 acres to be used for housing units. This land could accommodate 250,000 units which would house almost one million people. That land should not be turned back to speculators, because if that happened we would find ourselves in exactly the same position five years hence when the land was sold at a fantastic capital gain.
The federal government should purchase the 50,000 acres of land and lease it under contract on bid to designers for housing units such as Habitat built for the 1967 exhibition. Entrepreneurs who were genuinely interested in providing such accommodation could be awarded contracts for the construction of 250,000 units to be leased. The units would be sold to the citizens but the ownership of the land would remain with the government, in this way we could cut the cost of the average unit from $10,000 to $20,000, as we would not be passing on the cost of the land to the purchaser. When an owner of one of these units decided to sell he would be required to sell the unit back to the housing authority. If he were allowed to sell it on the open market the price would be anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 higher with a substantial capital gain. This should be discouraged, and this could be done by requiring that the unit be sold back to the housing authority. The owner would be allowed, in addition to what he paid originally, a certain amount related to the increase in the cost of living, plus an amount for any improvement such as a patio or some other substantial change to the unit. There would be no capital gain. In this way we could keep at least the cost of that housing within reasonable limits.
I might say in passing that there is one government in this country which has started to move in this direction, and I refer to the province of British Columbia. I found out recently when speaking in the city of Kamloops-I was not aware of this fact before going there-that the government of British Columbia had turned over 40 acres of prime downtown land in that city for housing on the condition that it be developed on a leaseback program of the kind I have outlined.
If we combined these two approaches, that is changing housing financing by making mortgage money available at 6 per cent, and developing an imaginative land bank system so the land would remain in public hands, we could provide housing for all those post World War II babies who are now adults with babies of their own seeking accommodation on the housing market. This could not be done overnight, but within two to four years this problem could be resolved. We should adopt these two principles; providing mortgage money according to the needs without worrying about making a buck, and providing land on the basis of need instead of for speculative gain. In this way we could remove, in the years ahead, a serious problem, at least for generations if not forever, and housing would fall in the category of being a social right, just as we now have medicare and education in that category, services that Canadians now rightly take for granted.

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Tetrault

speechtext:
I am most delighted today, Mr. Speaker, to be able to express my views and those of my electors. The Speech from the Throne contains many words about social security. We do not seem to know too much about social security, but I think a responsible government in a free society would find it very easy to apply the principle that everything physically possible and desirable should be made financially possible.
This principle was applied during two world wars, the first from 1914 to 1918 and the second from 1939 to 1945. We never stopped the wars because we had no money, and I am sure that if a war broke out tomorrow we would be able to find all the money necessary to defend our country. However, once the war ended, I am sure the government would then again suggest that we tighten up our belts.
Both the Conservative and Liberal parties were elected with the financial help of large corporations. Once the old parties are elected they must first serve those who elected them, and this is detrimental to the labour force in Canada, or the little man.

Mr. Speaker, these were the words of James A. Garfield, a former President of the United States:
He who can control the money supply of a country controls the trade and the Industry of that country.
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the brave member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). He certainly has very good ideas to help those having housing problems and what have you. He said that the banks were making very large profits, around 85 per cent in 1973. I will come back to this subject later, Mr. Speaker, and give some figures. This may be somewhat monotonous, but I would appreciate having them printed in Hansard to open the eyes of my knowledgeable colleagues.
Mr. Speaker, on February 24, 1974, during a CBC interview with Mr. Andre Payette, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked the following question, and I quote:
Nevertheless there is in Canada at the present time one Canadian out of four whose annual income is lower than the threshold of poverty. While solving the problems of tomorrow, what is being done to settle our current problems?
Replying to that question, the Prime Minister admitted that there were too many poor people in Canada and I quote him:
I have always stated, and it is the point of view of the Liberal party, that Canada is an extremely rich country; its natural and human resources make it one of the most fortunate countries in the world. So we do not suffer from a shortage of resources, but we do have a distribution problem.
Mr. Speaker, for more than 30 years in the House, the Social Crediters have been suggesting that our monetary system is deficient, that it must be changed, that action must be taken to improve the fate of the poor in Canada.
When the first citizen of the country admits that there are poor people in Canada in spite of our prosperity, Mr. Speaker, the Social Crediters are not surprised, because in such a system as ours leading us into debt, it is impossible to get out of the hole.

Canada's public debt is continually increasing: 18 years ago it was $17,951,491,464 and in 1973 it was $51,717,700,000. Provinces and municipalities are also overburdened by debts and, Mr. Speaker, I know what I am talking about because for six years I was mayor of Val-d'Or and our greatest problem then was always the matter of finance.
At that time we were not wondering whether we had any equipment or men, but rather where to find money. Today, in 1974, the same problem is recurring. The more things change, the more they are the same.
Mr. Speaker, here are a few statistics concerning 1973: direct and indirect municipal debt: $8,421,273,000; yearly interest: $452,983,000. The provinces have a debt of $17,054,997,000; the interest they have to pay amounts to $566,185,000. Canada's national debt totals $51,717,700,000 on which we pay interest costs of $2,260,600,000 and this finally works out to $77,193,970,000 all told. Canadians must pay yearly interest costs of $3,170,771,000, which represents a grand total of $9 million a day in interest for the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder where we are going with such high interest costs, which must be paid by every Canadian. If my memory serves me right, every Canadian must pay $110 a year toward the national, provincial and municipal debt.
Mr. Speaker, how many bridges, miles of road, hospitals, schools and public utilities are not provided for the population because of this? These $9 million a day add to the wealth of financiers while the taxpayers continue to wait for the public utilities to which they are entitled and for which they have paid through their taxes.
The governments that allowed the public debt to increase uncontrolled are responsible for the useless spending of $9 million a day, the cost for servicing the public debt alone. This money should be used to meet the needs of Canadians rather than to add to the wealth of financiers.
Mr. Speaker, in 1970-71, the Canadian government lent $65,900,000 to the province of Quebec. Similar loans were granted to the other provinces under the same conditions.
Over 20 years the province of Quebec will have to pay the capital and interest, an amount of $162,900,000, that is about three times the total amount of the loan.
Mr. Speaker, those are figures that will give Quebecers food for thought and I am surprised that here, in this House, every time I address my colleagues concerning the monetary system, they do not seem to be interested nor to understand.

Mr. Speaker, the Social Crediters have repeated and will keep repeating several times that we ought to grant interest-free loans to finance public developments.
The only way to end the catastrophic indebtedness of municipalities, provinces and the federal government is to finance public developments through interest-free loans.

If there is logic in that, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what it is.

Mr. Speaker, there have been occasions in this House when I have taken advantage of the throne speech debate to be, what one on the other side of the chamber might term, hypercritical. But let me assure everyone that I have no intention of doing that today. Of course, there may be some regrets on that score. There are some important matters of government policy, and one or two other matters related to my own province, to which I should like to make reference, and I am delighted to see my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), in the House on this occasion.
First, I want to associate myself with hon. members who have already spoken in this debate and who offered their congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply. It was interesting and encouraging to note that both of those hon. members emphasized the plight of the less fortunate and deprived peoples of the world. While listening to them I was reminded of the old adage which says that if the problems of everyone in the world were put in one great heap and you could take back any person's problems you liked, chances are you would take back your own problems. Perhaps that is not entirely true in a world in which disparities are widening. However, it is true enough for us in Canada to recognize that, in relation to the other peoples of the world, those described by the mover (Mr. Stollery) and seconder (Mr. Pelletier (Sherbrooke) ) in this debate, our condition is nevertheless one for which we should be extremely grateful. In fact, if we were to take that theory of putting all the problems together and apply that to countries, I suspect there is not a Canadian alive today who, seeing the problems of virtually every other country on the face of the earth and given the opportunity to trade Canada's problems for those of other countries, would not willingly take back our own. I think this is another reflection of how successful and fortunate we are.

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
We can say this without being smug or narrowly nationalistic, and also while being fully conscious that despite our good fortune, relatively speaking Canadians have severe difficulties of their own that continue to impede the basic objectives that I am sure all members of this House hold in common with the great majority of their constituents. One such goal that has been pursued by every Canadian government in history has been the reduction of regional disparities. There are probably more laws on the statute books, and more programs in both federal and provincial departments and agencies, relating to this subject in one way and another, than to any other. It could hardly be otherwise given the makeup of our country and the continuing necessity to combat a broad spectrum of natural forces in order to maintain and strengthen national unity and ensure for all Canadians a fair share of our national bounty.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to turn this into a philosophical discourse, but I hope that hon. members will permit me on this particular occasion to remind this House that in just over three weeks' time my native province, Newfoundland, will celebrate the completion of its first 25 years of confederation.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Welcome!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Having been very deeply involved in a variety of ways in the events leading up to that historic joining of our two countries, this may he an appropriate time to tell this House what we as Newfoundlanders expected from the union and the extent to which our expectations have been realized. Of necessity, these are personal observations, but I believe they will reflect the views of a great many people of my province. Today, all but a handful of us are happy to be Canadians.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That includes, I might add, those who favoured confederation and that substantial minority, including myself, who had doubts about the wisdom of union and who fought and voted against it. Incidentally, it says something about the rapidity with which time passes to observe, and hon. members may be interested in this particular statistic, that today, just 25 years after the event, no less than 60 per cent of our Newfoundland population has never known anything but Canadian citizenship. Put another way, only a rapidly shrinking 40 per cent of the people of our province can recall our days of independence. That is truly, I think, a really remarkable and, in some cases, frustrating reminder to us all of how fast time goes by.
It is satisfying and somewhat ironic that today I find myself a member of the government of Canada, a proud Canadian and even prouder member of this House of Commons and that I find myself the minister who has been given the primary responsibility for dealing with regional disparity, the problem which perhaps more than anything else, brought Newfoundland to accept union with Canada in 1949. The promise of that day was that our partnership offered us greater hope for the realization of

our aspirations than if we remained outside the mainstream of Canadian life. Today, although much remains to be done, I say, without serious qualification and with a great deal of satisfaction as one who describes himself as a Canadian not by birth nor by conviction but by conversion, that confederation has been good, extremely good, for Newfoundland.
Of course, Newfoundland is not immune to the impact of the revolution of rising expectations. In material terms, however, the condition of the Newfoundland people today when compared to that of 25 years ago-and I am sure the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) would agree with me in this-is so vastly improved that had such gains been forecast even by the most enthusiastic confederate of the late forties, the unanimous judgment would have been that he was certifiably insane. The evidence of this progress is everywhere, but a single example will suffice. In the current year, 1974-75 the Department of Regional Economic Expansion alone, will spend, in Newfoundland, more than twice the total budget of the province in the first year of confederation. That gives you some idea of how dramatic has been the growth.
It is not difficult to see why the great majority of Newfoundlanders are avowed federalists; why we believe in a strong central government and that the whole is more important than its parts. This is not because Newfoundlanders wish to have their hands forever in the federal till. Being a proud and independent race, we long, indeed pray, for the day when ours will be a have, rather than a have-not province. That day, however, is not yet; and until it comes the commitment to our fair share, implicit in the terms of union, must be honoured. I am happy to say that this government recognizes and accepts that responsibility and I pledge it will continue to do so.
It is not an easy task. Economic and social progress are relative. Although we have shared in Canada's prosperity and its successes over the past quarter century, Newfoundland was so far behind, there was so much catching up to do that the problem of narrowing the gap, of coming closer to standards taken for granted in many of the more senior regions of Canada has been frequently frustrating and always difficult.
Of course, we are not alone in this dilemma. Regional disparities continue to plague many other areas also; areas that have belonged to the Canadian family for a much longer period than has Newfoundland. No one is more aware of this fact than I, especially because of my present responsibilities. I hope, within the time limitations of this debate, to give this House some of the strategies that I consider appropriate, at this point in time, for dealing with regional disparities. Before I do, however, I would like to make one further comment on the attitude of most Newfoundlanders toward confederation. I ask the indulgence of the House in this regard because I want to get it on the record.
I have said that our expectation is, and always has been, that we will be treated fairly. We can ask for no less for all other Canadians. This is true, whether we are speaking in economic or cultural terms. We were a distinct group, with our own traditions and heritage for more than 450 years before joining Canada. We are determined to retain that individuality and, in large part, I believe, we have been
March 7, 1974

successful. I believe, therefore, that we as Newfoundlanders, can understand and support the special aspirations of other groups and provinces, such as Quebec, when they seek equality of opportunity and the preservation of their distinctive characteristics. In one way or another, each of us in Canada is part of a minority and this is good for Canada. But distinctiveness in matters that are important to us, is no barrier to a strong federalism. Indeed, it can strengthen Canada as a land in which each of us respects and supports the rights of the other.
I will turn now to some specifics with regard to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and some of the new approaches that we are adopting. The statement that economic disparities pose a threat to national unity has become a cliche; but it is true that eliminating these disparities is, as it always has been, one of our most difficult challenges. The approach this government has adopted is achieving results, some remarkably good. But, I am the first to admit that there is more that needs to be done. From time to time I have told various committees of the House of the general policy approach my department is adopting. If time permits, I will review these details later.
First, however, I believe members will be interested in proposed changes in the implementation of the Regional Development Incentives Act. This act, which became effective July 1, 1969, has been one of the instruments by which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has sought to improve employment opportunities in slow-growth regions of Canada. Some of the records with regard to its achievements to date, its weaknesses and some of its failings, were published in the spring. Members have had ample opportunity to discuss them. I have welcomed suggestions from the various corners of this House as to how changes ought to be made and I believe that what I have to say will indicate that I have been receptive to a great many of those suggestions.
I turn, first of all, to the question of decentralized administration. Like all the other programs of my department, the incentives program will be administered out of ten provincial offices and four regional one rather than centrally, here in Ottawa, as has been the case heretofore. All projects will be evaluated in the provincial offices, with decisions on most smaller cases being made there. The delegation of authority will seek to maximize the responsibility of the provincial offices in the management of the program. The regional and headquarters offices will provide support in evaluating large cases or difficult ones when this task is beyond the resources of the provincial office to undertake. Most large cases, and those involving technical or complex considerations, will be referred to an advisory board on industrial incentives which will now be composed of federal officials from other departments as well as from DREE. I might say that, after reviewing this matter, it was not proposed to have representatives of the business community, however respectable, on the board which was evaluating incentive programs of this kind. This will now be done internally, with various inputs from the various departments to the government.
This decentralized form of administration will provide applicants with increased service, as they will be able to
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
walk into provincial or regional departmental offices and discuss their applications with the incentive officers handling them. That, coupled with a more selective analytical approach aimed at reducing processing time, will provide applicants with decisions about their projects quicker than under existing arrangements. Again, this has been asked for widely, both in this House and outside.
The changes being introduced will call for the amount of the grant to be based on a standard formula according to the region and type of project. Here, again, I suggest there is a marked and distinct improvement over the old arrangement. In the Atlantic region, for instance, and this,
I suggest, will be extremely important to the hon. members concerned, new facilities and expansions to produce new products will be eligible for assistance based on 25 per cent of the approved capital costs for buildings, machinery and equipment. This is something which I wish to bring to the attention of members, particularly those from the Atlantic provinces, because it involves a change in the method of payment for the number of jobs created.
Under the new scheme of things, we will provide 25 per cent with regard to fixed capital costs, plus 30 per cent of the average wages and salaries in the second and third years of operation. Up to now, the incentive per job has been based primarily on the number of jobs which have been created and has not had much connection with the pay rate for that particular job; so that theoretically at least, if the job paid $75 per week, the incentive was virtually the same as if it paid $150 per week. Under this new scheme we are taking a justified step to encourage enterprises in the Atlantic provinces in particular to pay decent levels of wages and we are saying, "The higher your wage bill is, the more return you will get in the form of incentive." We will do the same thing in other designated and special regions, and they will receive the same level of assistance except that, for obvious reasons, since wage rates tend to be higher outside the Atlantic provinces, the percentage of wages and salaries to be used in calculating the incentive will be 15 per cent rather than 30 per cent.
These new arrangements differ, as I said, from those under the old program, primarily in that there was no standard formula on which assistance was based. In a rather general way that assistance was based on a great many fuzzy criteria, if I may use that expression. Now, the applicant will have a much better awareness of the level and degree of assistance which he will be entitled to and, also, he will be able, in the great majority of cases, to get that assistance on a much more rapid and assured basis than has been the case up to now.
I should say a word about modernization and expansion with regard to producing more of the same product. In the case of a fish plant, say, which does not have the technique to create a new product line, the level of assistance will be at 20 per cent of the approved capital cost of plant and machinery, regardless of the designated region in which the facility will be located.
I wish to move on, because there is so much to say in such a short time. On the question of relocation-and this is bothering a number of people-it certainly was not our intention to move available jobs around the country. We have tightened up the regulations and we will demon-

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
strate in precise language, when they are promulgated, that although our current regulations exclude an incentive in an instance where a project would simply transfer existing jobs from one location to another within a designated region, the regulation change applies this constraint to all of Canada and makes incentives contingent on any plants of the applicant or parent firms manufacturing similar products anywhere in Canada continuing to operate at the same level as at the time of the incentive application. This will be welcome news to many who feel that under some circumstances, perhaps, shifts were made within the Atlantic provinces or within designated areas in order to take advantage of the grant provisions.
I will turn now to minimum capital costs. We have had many representations to the effect that the floor or minimum which we were prepared to consider for incentives was too high. One of the major features of the revised program will be the introduction of incentives for smaller projects. In line with government policies I and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) have seen what we could do for small business. We have discovered that there have been many worthy projects put forward to the department under the old program that did not qualify because their capital costs were lower than those prescribed by the regulations. I think hon. members should note that the figure is $60,000 in the case of a new operation and $30,000 in the case of an expansion.
In the case of a new plant or an expansion into new product lines, which is virtually the same thing, these costs must normally total $60,000. We will be reducing that to $25,000. To make it more flexible still, in the case of that kind of new operation the costs involved may be either $25,000 or there may be the creation of five additional jobs. So, we will be able to work with the small businessman in the manufacturing and processing sector in particular, in order to try to encourage that type of enterprise. We will also reduce the figure to $25,000 for straight expansion of existing product lines. The reduction in that case, from $60,000 to $25,000, is not so great. We have simply brought both into line at $25,000, for obvious reasons.
I now turn to another interesting and useful change we will make in the regulations. Again, I hope this will demonstrate that I have been listening to what hon. members on the committee and in this House have been saying. We will bring in a new program providing for an incentive grant which is to be repayable under certain circumstances. This will overcome special problems encountered in several types of projects. One type involves projects which will be very profitable if the products are quickly accepted by the market. Where the government risk is considered worthwhile, an incentive may be provided with the condition that, if certain levels of profitability and other performance stipulations are met, the incentive will be paid back. This is an example of new flexibility. In looking at the profit position of a particular applicant, it might be very difficult to justify an outright non-repayable grant, even if it could be demonstrated that the project itself is worthwhile.
Even large and often profitable companies find themselves in cash flow difficulties, which may lead to the abandonment of a project or to delay in its implementation. This provision will enable us to say to a manufactur-

er or processor or company to which this will apply, "We will provide you with the incentive; but, if your profit projections turn out to be correct, then there appears to be a case for recovering these moneys at some point when you are on stream and your balance sheet shows that you no longer need this form of assistance. I hope we will be able to cope with certain other cases by using this technique.
Another type of project might not be able to attract sufficient financing at reasonable rates while, on the other hand, an outright grant might not be considered appropriate. In such an instance, a loan guarantee might be given if a suitable lender is available. However, where a lender is not available or the project might be lost because competitive funds are not available elsewhere, an incentive with specific provision for repayment might be a suitable instrument. Again, projects which might not have received an incentive can be assisted. I believe they can be assisted in a way which is consistent with our view that, while we wish very much to see industrial development take place in the slower growth parts of the country, we do not want, and I do not believe there is any necessity in some .nstances, to simply make public funds available as a gift. If the project is as good as the promoter says it is, surely the logic for some form of repayment, continued expansion or some other justification might deserve merit.
I want to touch on a few other modifications. We are going to change the qualification so that leased assets for incentives can be covered in certain cases. The forest industry, for example, often has a very large investment in terms of leased assets. Therefore, in order to accommodate the applicant, we will now embrace these, something we were not capable of doing before because they had to be fixed assets in the literal sense of the word. Something else we are going to do is adjust the list of eligible assets to include certain off-site assets employed exclusively for the operation. Here again I am thinking in some respects of the forest industry and some aspects of other types of manufacturing industry, for example transportation vehicles used between separate sections of the same facility. It seems to make eminently good sense to include these in the calculation of a grant.
There will be an addition of a few new activities to those already eligible for assistance. We discovered in some instances the definition of manufacturing and processing had to be broadened to some degree. I may say I am open to other suggestions beyond the examples I am giving today, but the type of thing is grinding, mixing and blending of fertilizer and feedstuffs, drying of hides, cleaning or drying of peat or Irish moss, certain transporting and merchandising activities and most types of concrete and asphalt mixing. These have now all been included in the program.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
There will be an increase in allowances for cost over-runs for payment. Members have asked me on occasion what we are doing with regard to the possibility that, with today's circumstances, estimates might well get out of hand in some respects and a project, after it had
March 7, 1974

been partially launched, might run into difficulty. At the present time we allow for a cost over-run of 15 per cent. It is now our intention to make that 25 per cent. This will take care of and answer that question that has been asked frequently about what we are doing with regard to compensating Atlantic provinces industry because of higher energy costs and things of that kind.
We are going to make changes in the provisions governing equity to provide greater flexibility in the time of payment of the equity participation. I believe this will be welcomed by certain applicants.
Another one members made representations on, and which I have come to believe is correct, has to do with the loan guarantee program and the magnitude of the loans and the minimums we will guarantee. This matter is of particular interest to tourist operators, for example. In this case, the loan program is available to certain new commercial undertakings and to new expanded and modernized manufacturing and processing facilities. In revising this, the guarantee fees will be lowered and the minimum capital costs required for a commercial facility to be eligible will be reduced sharply from $252,000 to $100,000. This will be very much of an improvement with regard to the number of people who can take advantage of the loan guarantee.
With regard to the payment procedures, we do not propose to make any change in the current requirements. That is, no monies are paid until I, the minister, am satisfied that the project is in commercial production, has been for a period of 30 days and the number of jobs are in place. In short, it will still be a question of proving that the project is operating before we pay them 80 per cent. The other 20 per cent, of course, is retained over a further period of time. I do not think there is any wisdom in making alterations to that.
In addition to the assistance which will be available under the revised incentives program in designated areas, that is those regions of the country which are marked as being eligible for RDIA, we have also taken into account the representations of members who have stated they cannot get incentives in their areas because they are not covered by the incentives program.
To date I have signed four general development agreements with the provinces, one with Newfoundland, one with Ontario, one with Alberta and one with Saskatchewan. I anticipate signing with Quebec probably next week, and with the other provinces before the end of the current month. Under these general development agreements, it will be possible for the federal and provincial governments to agree to support a major development opportunity in any area, whether it is in the designated section or not, provided the two governments are satisfied it will make a worthwhile contribution to the economic development and improvement to that area. I am sure the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) will welcome that particular piece of news.
I would like to say that I am very pleased with these changes in the incentives program. They have been worked out in consultation with the provinces, and will make that program a more effective instrument in our regional development efforts. The date on which they will be implemented will be announced as soon as final
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
arrangements for the transition from the old program are completed. Hon. members will appreciate there is a problem of getting from one program into another. It should not be more than a few weeks. Of course, before it becomes official, it will have to be gazetted, but that is all that remains to be done.
As for the general policy changes, I am very happy that the new approach has been, and I do not need to qualify this, universally welcomed by the provinces. As hon. members know, I have been back and forth across the country and there has been legitimate and, I believe, mutually satisfactory consultation on a wide range of matters, not simply the incentives program with which I dealt in detail, but the whole question of how we will approach with each province what they see as their priorities in terms of reduction of regional disparities and the improvement of slow growth areas.
One of the important discoveries, perhaps that is not too broad a word, that has emerged from this or has certainly been reaffirmed by this exercise is that a blanket program which falls with equal weight in each area of the country is clearly not the most rational approach. Individual governments have individual priorities and see their province proceeding in a particular way. Therefore, on that ground alone there is the necessity for us to the best of our ability to accommodate what provincial governments legitimately set down as their goals and objectives.
The second point is in a country as vast as ours, the opportunities vary markedly as to their size, availability and type. I will give hon. members just a few quick examples.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all, on behalf of my constituents in Medicine Hat, offer warm congratulations and best wishes to our newly-appointed Governor General, His Excellency Jules Leger, and to his most gracious wife, Madame Leger. I should like to assure Their Excellencies that a genuine western welcome, even a southern Alberta welcome, awaits them whenever they choose to visit Medicine Hat.
I should also like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Stollery) and seconder (Mr. Pelletier) of the Address, with particular reference to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) whose speech I enjoyed very much.
There are two subjects I wish to deal with this afternoon. The first is a very important local issue-indeed, in many respects it is truly a national issue. I refer to the closure, recently announced, of the defence research establishment at Suffield. Second, if time permits, I propose to make a review and assessment of the serious and immediate crisis confronting the Canadian cattle industry.
Mr. Speaker, Friday, February 22 was a bad date for the city of Medicine Hat. I am referring to the announcement by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) that the defence research establishment at Suffield would be phased out. On that date, too, the minister announced that a new defence research establishment would be established in the Winnipeg area, representing a capital expenditure item of $11.5 million and an annual maintenance cost of $6.5 million. In the government announcement it was stated that the new facility at Winnipeg would not mean any increase in the defence research budget since both funds and personnel would be transferred from other defence research establishments. With the greatest respect I suggest this new announcement means another $11.5 million of taxpayers' money, plus the operating costs, and is indeed a substantial increase in the government's budget. I think it is important hon. members realise that the facilities being replaced have a probable total capital value of some $40 million.
Let me briefly review the history and background of the Suffield research station, because I think it is important to do so. These facilities were created during the second world war as an army base. The station was formed through the acquisition of about 1,000 square miles of farm and ranch land along the west side of the South Saskatchewan River. The headquarters are located some 25 miles northwest of the city of Medicine Hat, just north of the village of Suffield. The Defence Research Board took over

the base in 1946. Headquarter facilities occupy an area in excess of 120,000 square feet of building space presently in use. The central laboratory alone occupies approximately
64.000	square feet. The Suffield Research Library contains
20.000	volumes. Building construction since 1947 has cost about $12.6 million. Prior to 1947, both the Canadian and British armies were involved in the wartime operation of the station. At the present time the Suffield payroll amounts to $2.5 million a year, nearly all of which is spent in the communities of Medicine Hat and Redcliff. This generates a tremendous amount of activity, business, social and otherwise.
The scientific, technological and research involvements of Suffield are legendary in Canada. Indeed, they are continental in their scope. Universities which have been associated with Suffield include the University of Alberta, the University of Calgary, Queen's University, the University of Saskatchewan and the University of Victoria as well as the Technical Institutes of Northern and Southern Alberta in Edmonton and Calgary. Industry in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom has also been involved in co-operative research because of the wide expertise available at this Suffield station. Computer facilities are available and have been used by agriculture departments.
One of the more spectacular and advertised activities at Suffield is the explosives testing program carried out by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, a program made possible by reason of the vast extent of the back-up area-1,000 square miles. Currently this area is being used for a United Kingdom army tank training program now in the third year of a ten-year contract. Some 184 families depend upon the research establishment for their livelihood. A good many of them have been there for more than 20 years. Many more Suffield residents are actively involved in the supply and service aspects connected with this institution.
In the period since the minister made his announcement not two weeks ago, I have received more letters, phone calls, telegrams and personal representations than I have received on any subject or issue since my election. They include representations from city council, the mayor's office at Medicine Hat, the Chamber of Commerce there, various unions on behalf of employees directly affected, and other organizations.
If, as the member of parliament for this area, I might summarize the views expressed in all these communications, I would do so along these lines. First, and foremost, this question was raised: if the research establishment in Canada needs to expand its northern operations and its activities in the field of search and rescue, as suggested in the announcement, if the government really believes in its policy of decentralization, particularly as it applies to the west, and if part of the Ottawa defence research establishment must be moved, again as indicated in the announcement, why should these activities not be added to those carried out in the existing excellent facilities at Suffield instead of building a new research establishment at Winnipeg for a further $11.5 million?
March 7, 1974

This afternoon in Suffield and Medicine Hat the minister's special assistant, Mr. Jim MacNicol, is hearing the views of all concerned about this decision to close down the research establishment at Suffield. In conversation with him before leaving for the west I asked him whether he was going to explain the government's decision. He quickly responded that he was making this special trip to listen to all who wished to meet with him, and I am sure that Mr. MacNicol will hear a very strong and united voice today asking that this Suffield decision be immediately reconsidered.
It seems to me that this decision is decentralization in reverse. By that, I mean it is moving from a 30,000 population city, Medicine Hat, to a 550,000 population city, Winnipeg, which actually is Canada's third largest city. This is reversing the east to west, and indeed the south to north, moves that most of us feel are so necessary to properly develop western Canada. Many of the letters I have received told me of serious personal involvements which will result, such as moving east when retirement plans have already been started in southeastern Alberta. The minister's reply to my question on February 28 suggested that I was aware that "the research establishment at Suffield has been phasing out for several years". Of course, I and the entire Medicine Hat community were totally unaware of this defence department of Defence Research Board decision until that day, February 22, which was less than two weeks ago. In retrospect, it probably would have been much better had we all been informed several years ago.
In summary, then, concerning this Suffield decision I most earnestly and seriously ask the Department of National Defence, and especially the minister of the department, to consider carefully the implications of this decision on the Medicine Hat-Redcliff community which I have the honour and privilege of representing. If improvements and additions are necessary in defence research establishments in Canada, why not at Suffield? I ask the minister seriously to consider this question.
I want to make a few comments about the cattle situation, but before doing so one of the letters I received on the Suffield issue suggested that perhaps I was more interested in cattle than in people. By coincidence, over the last two weeks I have also received almost as many communications on the fat cattle market crisis in which this industry is presently involved. These letters have come from a very wide cross-section in both western and eastern Canada. Because it is a national issue and because I have been spokesman for the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, I should like to comment on the current cattle situation.
For the second time within the last six months a fed cattle market crisis has occurred in Canada due primarily to the direct and indirect involvement of last year's freeze on beef prices in the United States. Live fat cattle prices in Canada have dropped eight to 10 cents a pound over the last three weeks, to a current level of about 42 cents in the west and around 44 cents in Ontario. Feedlot costs of gain in the west are 55 cents to 60 cents a pound, and probably a little lower in the east. Actual cash losses per head on most fat cattle sold over the last three months range from $100
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
to $150 per head. This is continuing and the situation is getting worse. In retrospect, the only way these losses could have been eliminated would have been to stay completely out of the cattle feeding side of our industry. Live fat cattle imports from the United States since January 1 have increased from 2,154 in 1973 to 29,114 in 1974, a 14-fold increase. There has also been a 50 per cent increase in the tonnage of offshore imports of carcass beef, exclusive of United States imports. This, of course, is the main reason for the dramatic drop in fat cattle prices today.
Our Canadian domestic marketing of fed cattle-by that, I mean grade A and grade B-are down 32,000 head, which is 10 per cent, for 1974 over the same period a year ago, that is, from January 1. However, we are not short of fat cattle in Canada. It is now apparent that there is a holdback from market of fat cattle both in western Canada and in Ontario. We should keep in mind that the largest calf crop in our history is about to be born both in Canada and in the United States.
Over the last three weeks between 7,000 and 8,000 fat cattle have been imported weekly, nearly all coming into Ontario. This is about two-thirds of eastern Canada's fed cattle weekly kill numbers. The week that is just ending tomorrow will likely see the largest number of imports for the year. A direct result of this is the extreme difficulty of getting bids on feedlot cattle, especially in western Canada. The packers are backing up because there is no outlet for their carcass beef in the east. Another result has been the extremely light deliveries in both east and west since practically no cattle are being offered. For example, today on the Toronto market there were only 600 cattle in total offered for sale.
On February 25, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association presented both a short-term and a longer-term recommendation to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie). The longterm approach has been suggested by long standing United States import quotas of 400,000 head per year, with appropriate quarterly quotas. In addition, the United States charges a 10 per cent ad valorem tariff on certain imported cuts of beef. Canada has no quotas on live cattle or dressed meat imports from any country. In addition, we have no equivalent to the United States ad valorem tariff.
The cattlemen have recommended that Canada should insist on a reciprocal, proportional quota system involving United States exports to Canada that would allow 40,000 head per year, or 12,000 per quarter. These figures are in the approximate ratio of the cattle populations of the two countries, which is ten to one. Because of the time lag to negotiate and to institute this quota provision, the cattlemen have also insisted on provision for a short-term, temporary tariff that would automatically increase with increased import levels. On Tuesday evening last, March 5, a seven-man delegation presented this proposal to our Minister of Agriculture in somewhat more detail than I have outlined here. After their presentation the delegation indicated considerable disappointment and frustration in that the minister did not seem to indicate any immediate and positive action.

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
I should like to say a word or two about this DES situation, since diethystilbestrol is again in the news. DES is now legal for use in cattle feeding in the United States. Implants of DES are presently available and in use in the United States. The feed additive form of DES will also be in use within 30 days when new supplies become available in that country. Canada's ban in respect of DES still stands and the Minister of Agriculture announced just a few weeks ago at the CFA convention in Saskatoon that it would not be lifted. Technically, I suggest that Canada has two alternatives: Either to re-licence the use of DES in Canada or institute a complete embargo on all imported fed cattle and beef from the United States. The cattlemen suggested that a monitoring or certification procedure on imports is not a practical method and would not be acceptable since it is literally impossible to tell whether an animal has been fed or treated with DES, and certification is begging the honesty of the industry in the United States.
By coincidence, the United States announced in a news report yesterday morning that their DES-free certification program was about to be launched. This announcement pointed up the fact that the United States is anxious to protect their very excellent export market for cattle in Canada, and also pointed up the fact that last year this market alone totalled some $141 million. I am entirely satisfied that the proposals of the cattlemen are both reasonable and workable and merit the full support of all hon. members in this House. Last fall during the first such crisis only the feedlot operators were hurt, while the cow-calf and grass yearling producers sold their cattle on very strong markets. Now, however, the entire industry is sharing the impact of the fat cattle market price, and this is why it is much more serious now than it was last fall.
If the feedlot industry in Canada is to survive, it must recognize that high feed grain prices will likely continue through the balance of this year and most of 1975. I suggest this is due to the world shortfall position on feed grains. The industry must also realize that there will be an unofficial fat cattle market ceiling established by consumer resistance at retail outlets. These two situations will dictate much lower prices for feedlot replacement cattle, perhaps as low as 40 cents a pound. We in Canada should not forget that we are a net importer of cattle and that almost all of our imports are fat cattle coming into Canada for slaughter. This has been the case for several years. Our imports come mainly from the United States, with lesser amounts, coming from Australia and New Zealand. The United States is also a net importer of beef and cattle, being probably the largest importer in the world.
The throne speech contained a very specific reference to our cattle industry and I should like to quote one sentence as follows:
-incentives to increase the production of livestock necessary to provide for Canadian and export markets.
The present and future life of the Canadian cattle industry is now seriously in question. Cattlemen are not asking for subsidies or handouts, but only for a fair and equitable opportunity to compete with our United States neighbours in this same cattle industry. Our own Canadian industry is a $1.5 billion industry at farm gate values. That is how

much it was worth last year and slightly less in preceding years. It is the largest agricultural commodity group in Canada today and it is worth saving. To save it we will require genuine understanding and some immediate action by government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to participate in the debate by referring to an entirely different subject, but the remarks of the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) this afternoon, and his attack on unemployment insurance, leave me very little choice but to answer some of his allegations. I do not intend to do so in a personal manner as I have never in the 12 or 13 years I have been in the House found it necessary to be abusive.
Before speaking about unemployment insurance, I want to follow tradition by paying tribute to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is significant that the mover, an hon. member from the greater Toronto area, reflected upon a comparison of affluence in Canada with the affluence of those countries vaguely referred to as being in the third world, whereas the seconder in a very deep and thoughtful speech reminded us of the poverty which still exists in Canada. Galbraith in "The Affluent Society" suggested that it is hardly beneficial today for politicians to ally themselves with those who are very poor, since in this industrial era, in north America particularly, the poor represent a very small minority, very inarticulate and very passive, and, quite frankly and bluntly, to be allied with them can quite often be a political detriment.
Poverty does remain in Canada. Those economists who think you can eliminate poverty by simply giving everybody a sum of money per week fail to understand the difference between being hungry and living in a poor environment. There are whole areas in Canada which, because of poverty, regional disparity, geographic location and the inability of having someone articulate on their behalf, find that they have substandard roads and substandard schools, because teachers do not want to move in and teach in these areas, as well as substandard medicine, because doctors do not want to go too far away from the centres of learning. So poverty has come to mean to too many Canadians more than just the absence of dollars and cents, but has become in reality the absence of opportunity. This parliament, including members on all sides, as I have no monopoly of concern for the poor, should remind itself periodically that there are still many thousands of Canadians whom one might consider to be in the poverty category rather than just hungry in the evening.
The hon. member for Hastings referred to a 1970 paper of which I should have been aware, having something to do with disability. I looked puzzled because disability has nothing to do with unemployment insurance but workmen's compensation. I can only presume he was talking about maternity and sickness benefits. I went back to my office and found about three and a half feet of paper on the subject, including the Mercer report and various discussion papers. The hon. member is welcome to go through them.
March 7, 1974

I know there were many estimates of what the cost would be of these particular sickness and maternity benefits. There have been papers prepared and sooner or later one will come out which might suit me or one might come out which would suit the hon. member, but very little will be proven. What has been proven is that previous to the Unemployment Insurance Act only 15 per cent of Canadian workers had any sickness benefits and only 3 per cent had maternity benefits-one of the prime recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. The hon. gentleman is entitled to his opinion. I think from my discussions with him that he is serious, so I respect him; but that does not necessarily mean he is right when he says that the trade unions are upset and are complaining about the practices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Let me say to him that next week when the Canadian Labour Congress appears before the cabinet we will learn whether they believe the commission is being operated properly, whether it is too lax, or whether it is operating too severely. This will be a very interesting meeting.
I do not usually quote economists because, as someone once said, the main purpose of the study of economics is to make certain that an economist does not fool you. There are, I suppose, as many economists as there are scientists, but unlike scientists they are the only people I know who can be well paid for anticipating something and then even more highly paid for explaining why their anticipation went wrong. Nevertheless, there are some good and valid economists. I think of the report put out by the C.D. Howe Research Institute which I believe is as independent an organization as one might find. I should like to quote one small section from a book put out by the institute written by Judith Maxwell and Carl E. Beigie:
In an earlier section of this chapter, we concluded that Canada does not have the plant capacity to employ all the labour available for work, and we also concluded that unemployment will rise in 1974 because of slower economic growth. One further conclusion that seems obvious is that Canadians should not consider the unemployed to be welfare bums. If, in fact, the unemployed are expected to work, then Canada has failed them by not providing jobs. This means that the country owes them an adequate income either from unemployment insurance, manpower training allowances, or the welfare system.
Many Canadians believe that programs making transfer payments to persons are already too expensive, and the Economic Council of Canada has urged the three levels of government to reduce the growth of these expenditures to an annual average of 11 per cent. While this is an admirable objective, it loses sight of three basic facts:
The high unemployment of recent years places a greater burden on transfer programs, as explained above.
The sophistication of modern medicine means that many ill, injured and aged people are kept alive when in other societies they would not survive. This means that the population of handicapped people is relatively larger here and, in addition, that Canada keeps them in greater comfort than do many other societies.
Transfer payments must keep pace with inflation. To set a target of 11 per cent a year when prices are rising by 8 per cent means that the country has made a very small transfer of "real" income. Once the transfer payments system is perfect-which it is not-
There is a footnote referring to the Special Senate Committee report on Poverty in Canada.
-the growth rate should be at the same pace as inflation. But the system needs dramatic improvement first.
The Address-Mr. Mackasey
In summary, then, the main policy response to higher unemployment in 1974 should be to provide either incomes, training or jobs in community work for the people who are effectively locked out of the economic system.
Mr. Speaker, you either believe this or you do not.

speechtext:
It is 1974. I think it is ten days old as everybody should know who is interested in the subject. It has been in every daily newspaper, except perhaps the Hamilton Spectator in recent weeks. The term "welfare bums" is a despicable expression. That it should be used in connection with the people drawing unemployment insurance or even welfare is nothing of which any Canadian should be proud. According to a study of health and welfare, and the study by the C. D. Howe Institute, perhaps 14 or 15 people out of 100 on welfare could work if work were available. People who do not work because of the absence of day care centres and those who are chronically ill, mentally retarded and those who are third generation welfare recipients, or unfortunate alcoholics are not the type of people who work even in this time of affluence, and rather than call them welfare bums or resent the $1.40 or $1.90 or $2 a week that we contribute to UIC or welfare, we should thank God we are not part of the welfare trap ourselves.
It is ironic that the first voice that should be raised in respect of an inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Commission should be from the construction industry. Anybody who knows anything about labour-and I know the hon. gentleman who speaks for manpower does-and anybody who knows about technological change in the Labour Code will know it has not cost this country one day of labour unrest but on the contrary has resulted in many settlements. Amongst the leaders against that particular legislation was none other than the construction industry. But, what industry depends more on federal handouts than the construction industry in general? Unemployment insurance is the greatest handout and subsidy to the employer in the construction industry of any industry in this country and I am sure they would be the first and the greatest opponent of the concept of merit training which would place the responsibility right on the employer in the construction industry to provide his workers with a guaranteed annual income or would at least cut down on the characteristic of the construction industry today which is if you lay the cornerstone at 1.30 you fire the workers at a quarter to two. The government will look after them through one of its programs.
A construction firm can go from 800 employees to a telephone answering service, a secretary and one architect while the boss suns himself in Miami as the federally sponsored project comes to an end. Perhaps the inquiry should not be into the Unemployment Insurance Commission but rather into the construction industry and the way

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Mackasey
in which these people manipulate funds from the government. They build at a time that suits them. They do not spread the work across the year and in this way avoid the responsibility for fringe benefits and for a guaranteed annual income or some legal obligation to their workers. The problem with unemployment insurance is that it is a complex piece of legislation and all members, including members opposite, I am sure realize and appreciate this.
In the act, I believe in sections 108, 109 and 110, there is reference to an advisory committee which has power to inquire. That committee did inquire in October 1973 into the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The final report of that advisory committee was placed on the table in October. It was a unanimous report. One of the signatories to that report was none other than the representative of the construction industry. I would welcome a public debate with Mr. Durocher any time he has time to spare from his lobbying from department to department to see what he can accomplish on behalf of the construction industry or what he can do to build up strength to reduce the federal sales tax on building materials.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), for whom I do not hide my affection and concern, perhaps because he is a fellow maritimer, has always shown concern for people, as well he should because in the years when he was premier of Nova Scotia the average unemployment rates in that province were 20 per cent, 21 per cent and 22 per cent, and these were acceptable and considered normal. But now he comes along and at a $100 a plate dinner the other night says we need an investigation of unemployment insurance, not to see if it is administered properly but to see if it contains disincentives to work.
I point out that this is an act which provides an average of $70 a week, or about $1.75 an hour. What are the disincentives in such an act into which the Leader of the Opposition demanded an inquiry when speaking before "poor" people who had to pay $100 a plate for their dinner? It was great stuff politically, but let him come down to the Verdun anti-poverty association and I will arrange a bean supper for him at 50 cents and he can ask those people what disincentive they find in unemployment insurance. They will tell him all they want is work, that that is all they are seeking.
To suggest that Canadians are lazier than Americans shows a distrust of Canadians, a distrust of workers. It is an insult to suggest that the average European, the average American or the average Canadian does not want a decent job, something that will challenge his initiative and be compatible with the level of education that we provide in this country. If we educate the children of the Atlantic provinces who previously may have been denied secondary education, or even high school education, for financial reasons and then call them lazy bums when they come out of high school and will not work in a tavern cleaning off the tables, we should remember that we ourselves would not do that.
But perhaps the policy of the Conservative Party is to go back to the days before we had unemployment insurance. I say read "The Lost Years," by Broadfoot, before advocat-

ing that. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I was out in that beautiful part of the country, Alberta, in Edmonton, and talked to some 700 people there. There were many who had lived nine years on welfare, others who saw their farms disappear in the dust bowl and others who simply packed up their belongings and abandoned their farms. Because they drew $14 a month welfare in those days they were not allowed a radio licence, a beer licence, and certainly not an automobile licence, in case some of that money may have been wasted on a glass of beer, in case they may have stayed at home listening to the radio, or in case they bought a gallon of gas to go for a ride on Sunday. I ask hon. members opposite, is that the type of Canada to which they wish to return? It is the type of Canada we will see if they continue this unalleviated harassment of unemployment insurance, particularly if they do not base their criticism on facts.
I ask the opposition to remember that the press of this country has intelligence and that the press gallery in this chamber is not for sale to the opposition, to me or to anyone else. Rather, it is an extension of the House of Commons. Instead of feeding more and more on the question period, members of the press gallery are doing their homework; they are delving into the situation and finding the facts. For example, in Saturday's Montreal Star there was an article by James Stewart, who used to be in the press gallery 10 or 15 years ago and who spent a week or two studying unemployment insurance before writing about it. This is what he says about it:
In the eyes of the Canadian Labour Congress and the Confederation of National Trade Unions, in fact the law is already proving too restrictive and punitive, offering few improvements over the old system for some workers, and leaving too much influence in the hands of employers.
It is too long an article for me to read it all, but perhaps I might read his conclusion first and return later to other sections of it.
It looks more and more as though the bosses who scream loudest about the unemployment insurance scandal are part of the scandal themselves. They're simply lousy employers.
Perhaps the inquiry people have been asking for should go beyond the ski bums and maternity claimants.
It should look deeply into the big operators in the cheap labour market, the companies that lay-off at will, using UIC as a crutch to protect their profits, as a subsidy to reduce their obligations in sickness and maternity benefits, and as a scapegoat for their own shabby employment habits.
I take my hat off to Jim Stewart who had the courage to point out what too many of us here already know. Then he writes about the case of a woman as follows:
A woman, growing older and a bit slow, was laid off from her office cleaning job. She got something like $35 a week in unemployment insurance benefits, but she was told she had to prove a daily active search for a job.
She did this for a few weeks. Then she complained to her member of parliament that her diligent and vain search for work was costing her, in bus fares, $8 to $9 a week of her $35 benefit. Outraged, he told her to go home and relax, and if she had any trouble to call him.
I might say that it was a Conservative member of parliament who went to her rescue. Why couldn't she get another job, Mr. Speaker? She was 59 years old and she was no longer productive for the firm that won a federal office cleaning contract. She just could not wash enough floors between midnight and 8 a.m. to provide a proper
March 7, 1974

income for that enlightened employer, so he finally dismissed her. She went on unemployment insurance. She complied with the regulations which say that you must be actively seeking work. This cost her $8 or $9 a week in taxi and bus fares and finally she complained, as she had every right to do, to her member of parliament.
One of the complaints we have heard from the hon. gentleman from Hastings is his inability to get information. He always asks, "What are we hiding?" Mr. Speaker, any information I get is public. There is the Auditor General's report of October 5, 1973, which can be obtained from the library by any member of parliament. Statistics Canada will give you the complete breakdown of disqualifications and disentitlements monthly if you ask for it. Then there is the annual report of the Unemployment Advisory Committee which was tabled on July 7, 1973. There is nothing that is hidden. What is really the problem is that too few people understand how the act works; too few people care; too few people have the courage to speak for the poor, because to speak for the poor in these reactionary times is a political liability, and there are too many people in this House of Commons who judge their success by their ability to get re-elected, and nothing else.
I have said many times, and I have written innumerable articles on this, that I will accept any amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act that will improve it. But I will not accept anything that will drive the poor people into the hands of unscrupulous employers, that will drive them into conditions that are deplorable and that are bypassed by inspectors who never get around to inspect such places, or that will drive them to accept work with employers who pay only the minimum wage or below the minimum wage. There are ample cases of this in the evidence already available.
Employees in this country have never been quite so well off. It was only a couple of years ago that we were crying about unemployment. Today we are bothered by too much affluence and labour-intensive industry cannot find people to work for $1.25 an hour in Prince Edward Island, $1.50 in New Brunswick and $2.25 in Toronto for the one simple reason that you cannot live in Toronto on $2.25 an hour.
Maybe I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, but we never hear very much when we ask the opposition: what would you do to improve the act? I come back to the same argument that I used a year ago. We can throw the fishermen off, if you like. By strict definition they are employed. If you want pure insurance of the private nature, I say throw the fishermen off who are employed, but I doubt if anybody on the other side of the House from the Atlantic provinces or from any province, if he has the slightest humanitarian instinct, will get up and make such a suggestion. You can throw out the woodworkers who work piece-work in the middle of the woods. They are self-employed. Why not make that suggestion if you want to save money?

earns $180 a week? We have studied the facts and here they are: he has a mortgage, he has car payments, he has life insurance payments, he has a child in secondary school. If he is thrown out of work at age 48 for the first time in his life, he can postpone such expenses for about three months. Is he going to quit a job that pays $180 per week or more to draw unemployment insurance of $107 per week, and not sure if he can find work again? Where is the disincentive? Would you drop the $1.33 and put that person on welfare, or would you raise the minimum wage?

What were the old rates? They were 50 per cent, non-taxable, in 1968. When you calculate the rate of inflation between 1968 and 1974, you find that the man drawing $107 is earning less, in proportion to what he was getting when he worked, than the man who was getting $53 maximum, in proportion to what he was earning when he worked. Most of that $2 billion went into the areas of the country which needed the money-the Atlantic provinces, northern Ontario, northern Saskatchewan, the province of Quebec and the Gaspe area, to be spent by the poor in the areas where it should be spent.

How many people know that the country is divided into 16 regions and in eight of them the limit that you can draw unemployment insurance is 23 weeks, and then you are thrown off if you happen to miss one of the blitzes for which we are very famous.
