Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members. I can understand people believing that the plan is abused, and I select no one opposite as a redneck or a reactionary. There are reactionaries in every party, but what comes out of a party is a consensus. The people who went on unemployment insurance in 1972 with eight weeks work represented 2.5 of all claims in Canada. That is what all the excitement is about-2.5 per cent, 11 weeks or less, 35,000 people. There were 1,800,000 who drew unemployment insurance benefits at one time or another in 1972, and 35,189 had 11 or less weeks of work. Incidentally, they stay on benefits for a shorter period of time than the person with 20 or more weeks. They simply want a chance; they want a job. They are marginal workers who come out of school with substandard education and want nothing more than to work. They work as long as there is a job available for them, provided the money is sufficient to live on. That is the plain fact of life.
The person in Toronto who complains about his inability to obtain workers is usually an employer who wants it both ways-to be in the centre of the most prosperous city in the country, to have minimal transportation problems,

because chances are he has no railway costs, and at the same time he wants the same type of labour at the same wages as if he were located thousands of miles from Toronto. He has all kinds of spokesmen in the House of Commons, but not too many people stand up for the poor because it is not politically advantageous.
Let me give one example out of many. I will not refer to those referred to in the Montreal Star since I do not know where those examples came from or how valid they are. I remember that in October, just prior to the election, the Financial Times carried great headlines stating that a lumber company had laid off 187 workers, and eight weeks later when they recalled the workers, none showed up. According to the article, the workers were on unemployment insurance. The company could have kept the workers for those eight weeks if it had realized that they would be needed for the production of lumber eventually. But when the company wanted its 187 workers back, they were not available.
One of the directors of the company, a learned senator, came to me-after all the publicity was over, of course- and we discussed the problems. I got him to give me the social insurance numbers of the 187 workers involved so that we could run them through the computer and find out who they were and if they were still on the unemployment insurance list. It turned out that 14 of the 187 were drawing unemployment insurance. The other 173 were working for competitors of the company which had originally hired them, or for companies in other industries. When confronted with these facts, the senator said he was sorry. There was no retraction in the newspaper, however.
Being short of workers, the company went to Manpower and Manpower officials went to the camp to find out what was the trouble. Well, there was not much trouble. You could earn $300 a week in lumber camps, according to Bob Neilsen of the Toronto Star. Your only problem was that the camp in question was 92 miles from the nearest town and how you got there was your own business. When you got there, you slept with 16 other people. If your chain-saw broke in the middle of winter, you repaired it outside. Oh, yes, you could make $300 a week if you were in the right strawberry patch; that is, if the lumber was of sufficient diameter. There was no guaranteed weekly wage, let alone monthly wage, since you were on piece-work, and som-times you could not work when it snowed or rained. And this company complained because it could not get workers. I am not talking about a company in eastern Europe; I am talking about one in Canada.
In contrast, there are companies in British Columbia and in Ontario which build decent accommodations for their workers, which permit wives and children to come with the worker, which guarantee a weekly wage and provide transportation. There is a waiting list of people who want to work for these companies for the kind of wages they pay. Let those employers who are complaining about unemployment insurance and welfare programs as being for the benefit of lazy Canadians look in the mirror and see their own faults. They are prepared to overlook their own faults very conveniently and to condemn those who speak on behalf of people who normally have nobody to speak on their behalf.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by adding my voice to the tributes which have been paid to His Excellency the Governor General. I am certain that all Canadians join in wishing him every success and fulfillment during his tenure.
I think this was an interesting day of debate on the Speech from the Throne. I listened to the previous speaker with a certain amount of amazement. The basic principle behind his speech seems to be that flattery will get you anywhere. He would like to move a couple of seats to the right, I expect. Trying to compare the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the disadvantage of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is gilding the lily somewhat.
I enjoyed the speech of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). He appears to be the happiest man in the House these days. He has joined a winner. He knows where he is, and he will be here long after some of the flowers opposite have wilted. I listened to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) trying to rationalize and defend the Unemployment Insurance Act. I suggest to him that he should get a little support from his ex-cabinet colleagues if he feels like coming here and being punished frequently by the party which turfed him out of cabinet, I suggest it indicates a streak of masochism. However, that is his problem and not ours.
I was much impressed today with the very eloquent address of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). I wish I could speak as well in my first language as he does in his second. I would not agree, however, with the content of his speech. It would seem to indicate that his department is out of control. He appears to think it is an unmanageable department. I suggest that is too facile an excuse. No department is unmanageable; what it needs is a good manager.
The debate on the Speech from the Throne is different from most other debates undertaken by the members of this House in that it offers an opportunity to reflect upon the general direction of governance in Canada. Rather than discussing the minutia or motives in a specific piece of legislation, we can reflect on matters and trends which are of general concern to the country and to its future.
As the member from Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) noted when examining the economic aspects of the debate, "the question of whether or not one is prepared to support the Speech from the Throne really depends upon whether or not one can decide from what is said that this government has the vision and imagination to solve the economic problems that are facing Canada ..." This is indeed our function in this debate, to consider the past achievements and failings of the Liberal-NPD coalition and then to study carefully the merits of the government's plans, extracting what policy there is from the rhetoric.
In addition, and probably of greater importance, we must consider the aspirations and anxieties of the Canadian people. We must consider the future and the problems it will bring in the widest terms, in economics, ecology,
March 7, 1974

sociology, demography, politics; indeed, every facet of man's social existence must be considered. For, Mr. Speaker, it is incumbent upon the members of this House to provide Canadians with the leadership they need for the coming decade and it is this debate which gives us the greatest opportunity to consider this, the task at the core of democratic rule.
How, then, are we to judge the fitness of this government to lead the country? It seems to me that we must do these things: first, we must examine the aspirations of the citizens of Canada and the problems which will face the country, considering especially the record of the government in understanding these hopes; second, we must examine the government's suggestions as given in the Speech from the Throne and evaluate them in terms of their ability to satisfy the nation's needs; third, we must judge the record of this government in terms of its ability to implement that which it has promised.
All three of these are necessary, and while the need for the first two steps in unquestioned, the third is just as vital. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) put it last session, "the question of trust and confidence is part and parcel of the question of credibility." All too frequently policies have been evaluated in an abstract political vacuum; too frequently we forget that it is a specific political party which has to translate broad objectives into specific legislation and which must supervise the executive implementation of that legislation. We must judge the government party, or should I say parties, in terms of its ability to do this.
Of this triad of necessary conditions for good government, empathy with the people, programs and ability to translate programs into well functioning government outputs, I should like to begin by considering briefly the last condition by examining the success the government had during the previous session of parliament in realizing the objectives which it set itself in that Speech from the Throne. In examining that document in light of the last 14 months of government action or, perhaps more properly, government inaction, we see that the editorial comment, "there is less to it than meets the eye," was indeed correct. Of the plethora of commitments undertaken then, some have been fulfilled; however, the resulting legislation has tended to lack any consistency or unity of design.
This is possibly best exemplified in economic affairs where the Liberal-NDP union has created as its illegitimate offspring an incoherent mass of band-aid bills, each doing something to alleviate the hardship of those caught up in the government's economic mismanagement yet none of them offering any consistent or broad attack on the causes of the country's economic ills. The laudable pledge in the throne speech that the government will "contain inflation" and "attain reasonable price stability," after inflation of 9.1 per cent in the last year sounds now like the bitterest irony.
Fourteen months ago the government had proud words on social security. There were as bases for action the "five principles which, taken together, comprise a statement of the government's commitment in respect of social security." What has been the reality of the legislation on social security? Nothing except incremental adjustments which have barely kept pace with soaring prices. Like the crea-
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
ture in "Through the Looking Glass" who said, "It takes all the running you can do to keep in the same place," I only wish that the Liberal-NDP coalition would not continue to ascribe such grand munificence to their enlightened social philosophy but would, instead, give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) his due. It has been his mismanagement of the economy which has created the absolutely compelling need for increases to prevent those such as old age pensioners falling further behind in their race with the ravages of inflation. Is this the "compassionate and equitable guaranteed annual income" which the aged and disabled were promised 14 months ago?
As a light and humorous footnote, were it not so callous toward those caught on fixed incomes, we may listen to the blustering of the NDP. That marvelous group manages simultaneously to take credit for the raise in old age pensions and avoids responsibility for the niggardliness of the amount. Being able to ascribe all that is good in an action to oneself, and all that is bad to another, is an exalted exercise in either egotism or double-think.
It was a peculiar spectacle to watch the Prime Minister and the member for York South (Mr. Lewis) arguing last Thursday as to who could take credit for last session's band-aid legislation. Neither of them wished to take any responsibility for bringing the country to an economic condition where such band-aid legislation is necessary. Their differences, I suppose, come down to "Who runs Canada?" If the member for York South can dictate terms for his support, then he can equally be blamed for not insisting on sound economic policies. If the Prime Minister is correct and the NDP are merely seagulls following his ship, then he alone should assume responsibility for the inflationary mess we are in. These two party leaders squabbling over credit for the goodies, whilst blaming others for everything else, does little to enhance the image of parliament. It is a sorry sight. To attempt to take credit for high incomes, and blame others for high costs, is simply dishonest.
While not agreeing with Prime Minister Harold Wilson-and let me now congratulate him on his victory and wish him well in his extremely difficult task ahead-I admired his honesty and courage when he stated, "One man's pay raise is another man's cost rise." We could do with more of that kind of candour in this House. I am not saying that wage raises are the only factor; profits, world conditions and, not least, government extravagance all contribute to high prices.
In the 1973 Speech from the Throne the government also spoke at length on the subject of housing. Whether the legislation which resulted will have a significant effect or whether, as with pensions, it only represents running to remain in the same place we cannot yet tell. What is apparent is that the legislation did not tackle the root causes of high housing costs, costs which preclude far too many Canadians from becoming home owners. Will the government's meagre palliatives do anything about the phenomenal price of urban land, the greatly increased price of building materials or, above all, the usurious mortgage rates? No, not until a coherent, inclusive program is enacted, for these problems are the result of economic and demographic problems which need to be dealt with directly.

Let us reflect briefly on the interrelation between inflation and the high cost of housing. If there is an inflation rate of, let us say, 8 per cent, will mortgage rates fall below 8 per cent? Never, for only a fool would loan money at a rate that would ensure his losing real purchasing power from that investment. What happens to the price of land? Unfortunately, it becomes more expensive when more of it is bought for speculation. During times of inflation it becomes a good investment for it is a classical hedge against inflation. This sets off a vicious circle, vicious, that is, for the hapless, prospective home owner as increased demand forces up prices, making land a better investment against inflation and thus causing greater demand, higher prices, and so on and on.
To be far, I must admit that the Liberals did not pledge themselves to a fight against these basic problems in housing, and in this they have lived up to their word for they have certainly not tackled these basic problems.
Let us now turn to the government's latest Speech from the Throne to see what promise it holds and to search for any new commitment to a more thoroughgoing and coherent approach to legislation. The first thing that strikes me is that the government has finally seemed to realize that inflation is a problem of very serious proportions. That is well and good; but what form does that recognition take? It is, unfortunately, in the form of an extended mea non culpa. One wishes that half the energy which the cabinet puts into finding excuses were directed to finding solutions. Here the government has seen fit to blame the sinister forces of international economic problems for Canada's inflationary ills.
Is there any mention of the vast increase in the money supply? Is there any mention of lack of a government supply policy? Is there any mention of the effect of an increase in government expenditure of 19.6 per cent? Is there any mention of the inflation psychology fostered by statements like those in the throne speech, that inflation is a matter largely external to Canada and, therefore, beyond the control of the government? The answer to all these questions is no. Instead, we hear only the repeated incantation; international forces, international forces. This excuse, presages, unfortunately, the absence of any effective government legislation to deal with inflation. If the experience of the last throne speech is to be believed, for the good of the country let us hope that the government will instead do something effective and that the Minister of Finance will study carefully the speech which the hon. member for Don Valley made to the House last Friday.
On the lighter side, the address also contains a number of sections which seem to be on the same order as being for goodness, motherhood and apple pie. I am sure that all members of the House are for "the producer must be ensured a fair income for his work", of "the consumer must be ensured a fair value from his dollar," or my favourite, "research to make it possible to increase production, improve quality and lower costs". Babbitt is not dead while the writer of that cliche lives. There seems to be a strong emphasis on things being reasonable or fair, but virtually nowhere are we told what this is to mean in terms of objectives or policies.

In reading the rest of the Speech from the Throne I am struck by the lack of any systematic view of what needs doing. There is a series of disjointed proposals. Each is of varying merit, although most are in some measure useful. However, they do not cohere. One cannot adduce from them any consistent approach or comprehension of the aspirations of the people of Canada. This is, I suppose, what above all else discourages me about the present Liberal government. It lacks direction. It lacks vision. In worshipping the exercise of power for its own sake, the government has not only lost touch with the people's hopes but also has reached a point where it even fails to comprehend the essential problems facing Canada.
I have been here now a relatively short time, 14 months, but sufficient time to form opinions about the ministers of the Crown. The ministers occupying the treasury benches seem unable to respond to or produce a call for action. Look at that front row. We see the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) who acted as a second to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) in his famous fight to keep tankers out of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. As the Leader of the Opposition said, "If that was a fight, we should get our money back." All pretence at even a token fight stopped, of course, when the Prime Minister declared that the tankers must go through.
Looking along the front bench further, we see the Minister of Transport who provided the layman's view about freight rates at the Calgary conference. At that conference there were only two people around the table who did not know anything about freight rates. Unfortunately, one was the Prime Minister and the other the Minister of Transport. This was embarrassing even to opposition MPs who were in attendance.
It has not gone unnoticed in British Columbia that the Prime Minister announced that the west was now to be officially considered as alienated and that steps would have to be taken to bring the western provinces back as the Liberals had done with Quebec. That message must have lost something in the translation, because the Minister of Transport almost immediately dictated that the airport in Victoria would become bilingual. Such hamhanded misinterpretations of the Official Languages Act makes it extremely difficult for the moderates in our country to prevail. I am only being half-facetious when I say the last person insisting on being spoken to in French at Victoria airport was reported to be Keith Spicer, and that was months ago. I do not wish to pursue that matter further, as in the present context almost any mention of bilingualism tends to exacerbate the problem. Perhaps I could close this subject by quoting Solzhenitsyn who said, "Intolerance is the mark of an inadequate education." There are, unfortunately, too many intolerant people on both sides of this question.
A little further along we find the hon. and affable President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and House leader for the coalition, although the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) may be entitled to some of his extra allowance for the position. In his position as House leader he has taken a leading part in the negotiations concerning redistribution. Another title might be, "How to set democracy back ten years." In this cause he produced "Redistribution, 1974 approaches and
March 7, 1974

perspectives." Other than the misleading tables attached to his production, I object most strenuously to his peculiarly selective quotations from Laurier, Borden and St. Laurent which give the totally erroneous impression that these statesmen were not strong supporters of representation by population. This is a time for Oscars and Grammy awards, and to the government House leader I bestow the George Orwell award for creative history for the year.
I listened to and read about the speech which the Prime Minister made in Toronto last night. His speech this year in the debate on the Speech from the Throne was much better than that of last year. However, I resent his using the House of Commons for a trial run of the speech he was to make at a fund raising dinner in Toronto later. He told the same jokes there as he did here. He addressed a well fed and well heeled group of the Liberal establishment whose loudest applause was reserved for his assurance that the status quo would remain. Small wonder they applauded. They are not only able to protect themselves from inflation but, indeed, to profit from it.
Looking further down the front bench, we see the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This minister is the one who professed total lack of knowledge of any diplomatic freeze between the United States and Canada, although it was being discussed publicly in the United States. In point of fact, the state department of the mightiest nation on earth refused for two or three months to accept any Canadian diplomat above the Canadian desk level, yet our Secretary of State for External Affairs knew nothing about it.
A little further down the treasury bench we come upon the charming and hon. Minister of Finance. I wish to pay him a compliment. He is a true House of Commons man. I enjoy his speeches, but that does not mean I agree with him. He produced a budget on February 19, 1973, over a year ago. His most famous statement was, I suppose, when he declared the following on that occasion:
This budget is aimed at reducing inflationary pressures in Canada and at offsetting the effects of past inflation ... It is equally essential to reduce the squeeze of rising prices on family budgets and the erosion of the hard earned savings of Canadians.
That budget promptly generated the most disastrous erosion of savings and the highest inflation rate in modern times. I also wish to comment on something the Minister of Finance says frequently. He discusses the people he has dropped from the tax rolls. However, this goes back to the days of Mr. Benson who, on presenting a budget on June 18, 1971, said:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of all the changes in taxation of personal income that I am describing tonight, 1,000,000 taxpayers who would otherwise pay taxes next year will be removed from the tax rolls.
The present Minister of Finance reiterated this on February 19, 1973, when he said:
Tax reform introduced some 18 months ago removed from the tax rolls a million Canadians.
Continuing, he announced that one of the main points of the 1973 tax legislation was that three-quarter of a million people were dropped from the tax rolls. This means that wandering around the country out of a taxable population of a little more than seven million, there are 1,750,000
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
Canadians who have been removed from the tax rolls. And I have never met one of them. I don't know where they are. I wander the streets and I don't go around deliberately in the areas where everybody pays taxes, but in the poorer sections of my constituency I have never run into anybody who has said, "Thank God for Mr. Benson and for the present Minister of Finance. I have been removed from the tax rolls."
I thought this sounded kind of funny, so I had the tax returns looked up and my sources produced the basic statistics, the reports of 1971, 1972 and 1973 which show that in the year 1971, when Mr. Benson made his famous million cut, there were 7,363,963 taxpayers. In 1972, a year later, when the million should have presumably been taken off the tax rolls, there were in fact more than 7,600,000 taxpayers. This is like the flim-flam trick that goes on in the midway-the three-card trick where sometimes you see them and sometimes you don't.
The fact is that in 1973 there were still more people paying tax than there were in 1971. This is a cheap political trick. I would have come close to being unparliamentary by saying the minister was deliberately deceiving the House, except I did not think for a moment that anyone was being deceived. I did not think anyone would believe him, it was so patently dishonest. I was surprised to read a newsletter from the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who quoted the figure of 750,000 being dropped from the tax rolls. He took credit for it at that time. So apparently the minister did deceive at least one member of the House. These people have not been cut from the tax rolls. They have done a little paper jiggery-pokery and probably claim that if nobody had had a pay raise during the year, about a million would have been removed. But everybody's pay went up, and they were not removed. I wish they would quit trying to deceive the country in this way.
However, the minister usually pays close attention to both the Leader of the Opposition and to the honorable member for Don Valley, and though he is a slow learner he has no scruples about cribbing, so we look forward to an improvement, hopefully, in his next budget.
Moving back toward the centre, we locate the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). It is he who suggested a 3 per cent raise in pay for civil servants at or near the bottom of the civil service pay scale. He never seems, to me, to have the image of a cabinet minister. To me he works and acts more like a business comptroller who has been probably lent to the cabinet by some friendly corporation to keep control of their more woolly-headed socialist members.
There are too many members of the cabinet deserving of condemnation for me to deal with them all at this time, but I should not let the second row pass unmentioned since there we find such ministers as the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) who appears to be trying to wind down his department. Perhaps he wishes to be the final minister of veterans affairs. Then there is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) who, when the price of bread went up, suggested that people quit eating bread. There is an historical precedent for this. When Marie Antoinette heard that the people were rioting for bread, she said, "Let them eat cake." I am

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
surprised the Minister of Consumer Affairs did not think of this.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Prime Minister had another alternative.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, he had another alternative suggesting a different kind of confection. We work our way along to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) who has clearly ordered, now, that if war breaks out he should be awakened, even if is before 8 a.m. We work our way along to the end of the second row, past several ministers who belong mainly to the low profile, "keep out of trouble school," and we end up with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). This minister said in his maiden speech that he hoped to become a House of Commons man. His abrasive answers, or non-answers, to questions have done little to establish any such claim. It is hardly fitting or proper for a minister to tell questioners that they should read his press releases or his speeches and not to expect to get an answer in the Commons. After all, this is where we are entitled to ask questions and get answers.
In his department, incidentally, there has been tremendous growth in expenditures. They have risen to $6,854 million. I notice that the Grit member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Poulin) has stressed the growing danger of the drug heroin. But, like most back benchers in the Liberal Party, apparently he has little influence with the government because despite the enormous increase in the department's expenditures, the funds available for the fight against the non-medical use of drugs have been reduced. This leaves considerable doubt in my mind as to the correctness of the priorities of the minister of health.
I apologize to those ministers I have missed. It is not that they are unworthy of condemnation, but there is such a dreadful sameness about their gaffes and their maladministration that one wearies. I would not want you to think, Mr. Speaker, that they are not well-meaning people. They are. They are doing their best, and it is regrettable and most unfortunate for the country that their best should be so mediocre.
As I talk to my constituents, I am worried also at the degree of their alienation from our central government. To people in British Columbia, the federal government is a long way away. To them it is not only far removed but unfeeling. Inflation, high prices, shortages, rising federal taxes and budgets are things which are apparently beyond influence, matters controlled by a government of strangers whose actions are no more responsive to the importunities of the man in the street in Victoria than is the weather.
I find myself having to counter the argument that the federal government is irrelevant, though it is a sorry and lame reply to have to say that it must be important since it costs every man, woman and child in Canada $1,000 a year; that it must be important because it is the main cause of inflation and resultant insecurity for all. But the things that are visible and relevant to the citizens are their streets, sewers, highways and schools. All these things involve provincial or municipal government. I believe we must try to bring our central government closer to the people.

The Speech from the Throne is almost irrelevant even as far as members of this House are concerned. How are we to involve the people if we cannot give them anything better than this poor excuse of a program for the session? Why not a Throne Speech some time which states precisely what the government intends to do about the main issues which concern Canada? One is tempted to attribute the government's timidity, when it comes to enacting more than remedial legislation, to lack of courage. But to quote Plato, "It is wisdom which makes courage, self-control and integrity possible, or, in a word, goodness". It is a disquieting thought, but perhaps it is wisdom that this government lacks. I fear it is so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I begin my participation in this debate by adding my congratulations to the mover and to the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. This is one occasion when people in the back rows get a chance to lead off. Maybe this should happen more often. I do not agree with much of what they said, but I congratulate them on the way they said it.
The Speech from the Throne lists a number of measures which the government says will be placed before the House. Many of them are measures which members of my party, as well as of other parties, have been advocating for a number of years. I, for one, along with many other members of the House, an anxious to see just what this legislation will be. We are anxious to find out whether they put their actions where their mouth is.
Before I deal with some of the items in the throne speech I want to add a few sentences of my own to the plea that was made by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on behalf of the senior citizens of Canada. I have yet to find a member of this House, of any party, who is opposed to the idea of reducing the pensionable age to 60, at least on a voluntary basis, so that a person who wants to leave the work force and retire at 60, or a person who has to leave owing to illness or for other reasons, can do so and be eligible for pension.
In addition to that, it seems to me we must now provide that the pension will go automatically to the spouse of a retiring senior citizen so that we put an end to the situation where thousands of couples in this country are living on one pension. When a man has reached 65 and is eligible for the old age pension, his spouse, if she is in her late fifties or early sixties and is not employed, should automatically become eligible for the pension.
Finally, while all of us welcome our accomplishment last session in getting the cost of living escalator clause built into the old age security pension, and we welcome the small increase-it was slightly larger than the Conservatives offered, but still small-to $100 a month, we must continue to take steps to increase the pension until it reaches the $200 a month level.
I compliment the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mack-asey) on his speech this afternoon. He was much better able to keep his temper than I would have been; I would
March 7, 1974

have used some of the words that he said he would not use. But I do want to ally myself with the words he used in regard to those who were trying honestly, legally and properly to draw unemployment insurance benefits. The problem here, Mr. Speaker, is not the myth of the ski bum or the loafer who is drawing unemployment insurance; the problem is that people who are entitled to draw unemployment insurance and should be drawing it are being disentitled by the thousand each week. This kind of witch-hunt being conducted by a frightened Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), in response to the rednecks and hardhats in his own caucus and in the caucus of the official opposition, is unfitting for a democratic government and democratic system.
Every member of this House has been swamped with phone calls and requests for help by people who have been disentitled to unemployment insurance benefits during the past year or more. I find, Mr. Speaker, that people are being disentitled because thay have been led into answering questions in a certain way during an interview and then conned into signing a statement in which they automatically incriminated themselves and caused their disentitlement to benefits.
I have no objection to a requirement that a person who draws benefits must be actively seeking employment. But I do object when overzealous officials of UIC go to the length of requiring a woman to refund $15 to the Unemployment Insurance Commission because she was honest enough to say there was one day when she was not available for work, and that was her wedding day. She did not get married until 6.30 in the evening, but UIC insisted that she send back $15 because she was unavailable for work that day. How cheap and "chintzy" can you get in a witch-hunt by a frightened Minister of Manpower and Immigration, some of his colleagues and members of the official opposition, to search out people who are allegedly drawing benefits to which they are not entitled?
This whole business about leading applicants to reply to questions and then to sign statements which under the regulations restrict them to a certain kind of job or amount of pay or location of work has been carried to an outrageous extreme, and I am glad the hon. member for Verdun made the speech he did today. I hope members of other parties will do likewise.
Items in the throne speech that we in the New Democratic Party are anxious to see legislated include, among others, the legislation that finally is going to set up a national petroleum corporation. May I say to my hon. friends opposite that we hope they mean business. This corporation must not be merely an agency whose efforts in research and planning, etc., are designed to do nothing more than aid and comfort the well-being of multinational oil corporations. This must be the beginning of a massive entry by the Canadian public, through public ownership, into research, exploration, production and distribution of oil and oil products. If the bill provides for anything less than that, I can assure hon. members on the government side they will have some problems.
The throne speech refers to an increased availability of feed grains. I am glad to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the chamber. If the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board mean
The Address-Mr. Benjamin
by "increased availability of feed grains" that more is available because the price on the open market and in the hands of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange is going to be cheaper, then I can assure both ministers that they, too, are going to have some problems. I hope that any measure brought forward to increase the availability of feed grains will provide that they are to be restored entirely to the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and that this jurisdiction will apply from the Atlantic to the Pacific. If the measure does not mean that or something like that, again the Minister of Agriculture and his colleague from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) are going to have problems.
The throne speech makes mention of "an agricultural stabilization plan to encourage rational production decisions", whatever that means. It also mentions "a prairie grain market insurance plan", whatever that means. I will say only this much about those two items. If one or both of them is designed to take the place of the misbegotten legislation that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board brought in in 1971, then it had better be much better than that legislation was.
I listened to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board on a farm broadcast a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, and you should have heard him. This is a man who could forget history, could rewrite history and could distort history that was only two years old. He made some remark about a few opposition members obstructing the legislation. Well, there were a few of us not only obstructing; we damned well stopped it going through because it was bad legislation. The minister conveniently forgets that the farm organizations were unanimous in their opposition to it, one of the few times when they have been unanimous about anything. He conveniently forgets the four reasons why we did all we could to prevent that bill from passing. If he forgets them again in this new legislation, then he and the Minister of Agriculture and other members on the government side are going to have some more problems.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board can distort the record all he wishes, but that legislation was fought and prevented from passing because the government was attempting to repeal the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board has now succeeded in doing that via the back door, by making sure there was not enough grain in store in the terminals at the end of the crop year so that the federal government would not have to pay storage costs under that act.
The minister now complains, and pleads with the farmers to haul grain. If he had kept grain in storage at Thunder Bay and Vancouver to 80 per cent of capacity at the end of the crop year last fall, he would not have to cry now for farmers to haul grain. However, he was able to save the government some money in that it did not have to pay its proper share of the cost of storing grain. He wanted to phase out PFAA, which has been done, but at least we got better crop insurance out of it.
There are two items which had better find their way into any government legislation in the form of stabilization bills. That legislation must include provision for some kind of escalator feature in respect of the increase in cost

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. Benjamin
of production based on net farm income rather than gross farm income. If this principle is not found in proposed government stabilization legislation, that legislation will be treated accordingly by the members of this party, members of farm organizations and others in this country.
A great deal has been said in the last few weeks in the press and in this House by spokesmen for farm organizations, spokesmen for the government as well as by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, in respect of the movement of grain. In this regard the minister, during the question period today and on other occasions, has blamed all the difficulties on the snow conditions. He will not admit it, but the Canadian railways were behind in grain movements before the first snowflake fell in Saskatchewan or anywhere else on the prairies last fall. They were behind then, and they are further behind now.
There is nothing new about this problem. It has occurred and recurred almost every year since the end of the second world war. Successive federal governments have refused to face up to the problem and deal with it in any effective way. We had a classic example forcefully brought to our attention last winter regarding this situation on the prairies, showing how incapable our railway transportation system is to meet the transportation needs of the country. They have never kept up with transportation requirements. To understand that this is the fact one need only look at the deteriorating condition of our railway tracks and consider the inadequate number of snowplows and locomotives to deal with snow conditions. Mile after mile of the lines of both railways in the three prairie provinces sat unused for six or seven weeks this past winter without a wheel being put to them.
To illustrate this point I would refer to what was said by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) yesterday. He said that 25 carloads of grain sat on one siding for almost 60 days. On a little siding in my own constituency, Adams, there were seven empty cars put in on January 29. Four of those cars were loaded on January 30 and three more were loaded on February 11. All seven cars are still sitting there. Four more cars were loaded yesterday by the elevator agent. He could not finish loading all the cars because the track was blocked with snow. I suggest there are thousands of carloads of grain on the tracks at various points which have been sitting there for weeks because the railways are incapable of moving them. Thousands of cars have been waiting to be loaded but the agents could not load them because they could not be spotted.
Both railway companies have decreased their mainte-nance-of-way forces, with the result that back tracks and switches have remained unshovelled and uncleaned for weeks on end. Snow fences are not only unrepaired; some have been taken down and never replaced. The CPR complained about having 19,000 miles of snow to plow in the prairie region this year as compared with only 1,000 last year. I would ask where their snow fences are and what has happened to their maintenance of way crews. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) complains that the railways thumb their noses at him and will not honour his requests. If the Minister of Transport has not learned by now that he must make the companies do these things, I suggest we need a new Minister of Transport.

Another item which is in the throne speech concerns steps to be taken to end any discrimination in freight rates. We must see that suggestion implemented. I never thought I would live to see the day when discrimination in freight rates came to an end, but it is in the throne speech and we are now waiting to get the legislation. We are anxious to see it, because we want to know what the Liberals mean by "any discrimination in freight rates". That statement which appears in the throne speech is pretty all-inclusive. If the government is really going to act on this, it will be a great day for western Canada and I am sure this will be of help to the people in the Atlantic provinces, in northern Ontario and in eastern Quebec. When that is done, it will be a magnificent day. I think I can even stomach the Liberals a few weeks longer just to see that legislation.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But how much longer?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let me mention one or two other freight rate items in order to be helpful to the Minister of Agriculture. He might want to use my suggestions when he is finalizing the drafting of legislation, or to strengthen his proposals to the cabinet in order to make sure the legislation does in fact do away with discrimination in freight rates. It now costs 19 cents a hundredweight to ship live cattle from Edmonton to Vancouver. If you butcher the cattle in Edmonton and ship it to Vancouver as dressed beef, it costs $1.39 a hundredweight. It costs $2.90 a hundredweight to ship livestock from Prince Albert to Toronto; but if you butcher the cattle in Prince Albert and ship it as dressed beef to Toronto, it costs $3.40. What is even worse, the cheapest way of sending a carload of steel from Hamilton to Calgary is to ship it from Hamilton to Vancouver and then back to Calgary. The rate from Hamilton to Vancouver is $1.85 a hundred pounds, but from Hamilton to Calgary the rate is $2.65 a hundred pounds; yet Calgary is 700 miles closer to Hamilton than is Vancouver. If the Liberal government's legislation cures these problems it will be a great day for people in many parts of Canada.
I should now like to turn to another matter having to do with freight rates. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board reopened this matter when he said in a speech he made in Winnipeg last August that possibly it is time to review and adjust the Crowsnest pass rate agreement. Whenever anyone makes that suggestion, whether it is the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt or an official of the CNR or the CPR, it only means one thing: the only way they will review and adjust the Crowsnest pass rates is upward. We have heard similar statements by the Alberta livestock association and the Palliser wheat growers. That would be selling out the grain growers of western Canada if we adjust the Crowsnest pass rates. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and officials of the railway companies have said a good deal about the low Crowsnest pass rates, but none of these people has mentioned what the CPR received as part of the deal when the agreement was made.
Let me tell you a little bit about what the CPR received. They received $11,000 per mile, for a total of $3,630,000, to construct the rail line from Lethbridge, Alberta, to Nelson, British Columbia, through the Crowsnest pass and the Kettle valley. That represented about 35 per cent of the
March 7, 1974

cost. That is a real example of free enterprise getting welfare. That makes the people on unemployment insurance look like amateurs. The CPR also received nearly four million acres of land in 1897 when the Crowsnest pass legislation was passed in this House, including the mineral rights. They received six square miles of proven coal land from the province of British Columbia. The coal was there. Several tens of thousands of tons were being taken out of that area in 1897. In addition to that, they obtained a little deal to buy 33 miles of rail line, including mineral rights, some small smelters and mines in Trail and the surrounding area. Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company was established as a result of the Crowsnest pass agreement. In the last 60 years they have benefited to the order of some $300 million as part of the deal.
If the Canadian Pacific Railway is in fact losing money hauling grain-which I do not believe-as part of the deal, then it has been more than compensated through the profits from mineral operations and a host of other enterprises, as a direct result of what the people of Canada did in 1897. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will relate this to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. He would have a better chance having the Ten Commandments amended than changing the Crowsnest pass agreement unless and until any increase in the Crowsnest pass rates is included in an income stabilization plan. We will have to have the income stabilization plan first and then maybe we will talk about the Crowsnest pass rates.
Certainly if the Crowsnest pass agreement is to be done away with, we will take the right-of-way, the buildings, the rails, the mines, the smelters, the profits and give them back to the people of Canada. If the deal is to be cancelled, we will cancel the whole deal. If they want to back out of an agreement which they signed which says "in perpetuity"-which is a long time-and they want to back out of the freight rates part, they can do so but they will lose all the rest of it. I think the government of Canada could have a nice time with the hundreds of millions of dollars from the mines and smelters of that area, which could be used for the benefit of the people of Canada and to provide old age pensions at age 60 from the profits.
I should like to say a little more about rail transportation, particularly as it applies to the Canadian Pacific Railway. What this company received as a result of the Crowsnest pass agreement has more than compensated it for the grain rates. In fact, the Crowsnest pass agreement provided for a rate reduction in respect of a host of other products from eastern Canada. I have yet to find out how that disappeared from the agreement, because those rates have been raised many times. That is a small matter compared to what happened in 1881. As we know, Canadian Pacific Railway received 25 million "suitable acres of land". I shall come back to that in a moment. It also received $25 million in cash. We thought that was the end of it.
One might read the legislation and the agreement of 1881 which appears in chapter I of the Statutes of Canada, an act respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. There one will find that the CPR received many more things. They received 213 miles of railway that had already been constructed by the government of Canada
The Address-Mr. D. J. MacDonald between Selkirk and Emerson. The agreement also called for the government of Canada to construct and turn over to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the lines required from Fort William to Selkirk and from Kamloops to Port Moody. There was not much left for the CPR to build. It received 25 million acres, including mineral rights, and $25 million in cash and some more. In the legislation it also received from the government and the people of Canada duty free entry for all the material required for the construction of that railway-the rails, the telegraphic equipment and everything else. Then they received massive exemptions in respect of property and land taxes. The legislation reads:
The Canadian Pacific Railway, and all stations and station grounds, workshops, buildings, yards and other property, rolling stock and appurtenances required and used for the construction and working thereof, and the capital stock of the company, shall be forever free from taxation by the Dominion, or by any province hereafter to be established, or by any municipal corporation therein; and the lands of the company, in the Northwest Territories, until they are either sold or occupied, shall also be free from such taxation for 20 years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
I read some of the debates of the House of Commons for that day. I find that one, the Hon. Edward Blake, had something to say. By the way, it turned out that the Conservatives offered so much and lost, and the Liberals came in and offered more for the Crowsnest pass agreement. The Conservatives offered $6,000 per mile, and the Liberals offered $11,000 per mile. In 1880 in the House of Commons, the Hon. Edward Blake had this to say about what the government of Canada was doing for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company:
The great mass of railways in this country have been constructed out of resources mostly provided by private individuals. Considerable sums have, from time to time, been given by way of aid or subsidy by the government towards the construction of some lines, but the main portion of the capital of these railway companies is private capital.
He went on to say:
-but the same considerations are not at all applicable to a case in which you say to some individuals: Gentlemen, we will give you as much and half as much again as is necessary to build this railway, and we will let you own it afterwards. It is not the work of private capital at all. These men will, for a little while, until they make some land sales, invest four or five millions which will be recouped to them within a very brief space of time, and then they will have this enterprise without having sunk a dollar of their own money in it, and will have millions of acres besides.
Mr. Speaker, that is some of the background and history of the Canadian Pacific.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to join with other hon. members in congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I think they both did a remarkable job and deserve great credit. I also wish to associate myself with the tributes paid to His Excellency the Governor General and Madame Leger. I wish them both a most happy and successfull mandate at Government House.
Ever since I have been in this House, Mr. Speaker, it has always been a pleasure for me to observe the dignity and

March 7, 1974
The Address-Mr. D. J. MacDonald the diplomacy with which you have carried out your very difficult duties. I am certainly happy that hon. members saw fit to re-elect you, and also the Deputy Speaker to preside over this new session. I offer you both my best wishes.
In my maiden speech in this House last year I said I was very honoured that the people of Cardigan elected me as their representative in Ottawa. It is now over a year since they gave me that privilege, and I must say that I find it more and more challenging and interesting to work on behalf of the people of Cardigan as time goes by. They have continued to show their complete support for whatever I have endeavoured to do for them. I think I can say in all fairness that they appreciate what has been done for them during the past 16 months. Needless to say, I look forward to many more months and years of working on behalf of those who elected me.
As hon. members know, last year marked the one hundredth anniversary of Prince Edward Island's entry into confederation. Although the seeds of confederation were planted in Charlottetown in 1864 and the dream became a reality in 1867, reluctant islanders waited another five years before finally joining confederation in 1873. Of course, we were extremely proud and happy to celebrate all three of those centennials with equal vigour and enthusiasm. In 1973, Canadians from all over the country joined islanders in celebrating their anniversary. The former Governor General and Mrs. Michener officially opened the celebrations on January 1, 1973. From then on it was a year of festivities and of various events to commemorate the historic occasion. We were particularly honoured that Her Majesty the Queen and Prince Philip could join with us in celebrating the centennial. This was certainly one of the highlights of an exciting year. For me the occasion was all the more memorable because Her Majesty spent a considerable amount of time in my riding of Cardigan.
We were also privileged to have the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the federal cabinet pay a visit to the island and hold a cabinet meeting in the historic Confederation Chamber at Province House. This was the first time the federal cabinet had met in Charlottetown since confederation. Needless to say, I was particularly proud to take part in that historic event. I wish to take advantage of this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to express, on behalf of all islanders, our most sincere thanks to all hon. members, and indeed to all Canadians who came to the island and joined with us in celebrating our memorable anniversary. I am sure that the hospitality and the friendliness with which you were greeted will prompt you to come again as often as possible.
Hon. members will recall that a comprehensive development plan for the island was signed in March, 1969. I will not go into the details of the plan as I am sure hon. members are familiar with it. However, I would like to point out that since the implementation of the plan, the number of people leaving the island has declined substantially to the point where we now have a real population growth on the island. This means that a whole new generation of young people can find interesting and challenging

opportunities on the island instead of having to move to other parts of Canada or to the United States.
I should also point out that the numerous DREE projects which have been, and continue to be, approved for the island are of tremendous help to our economic development. I think the decentralization program that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) is now carrying on for his department will make it still more effective.
Another point that I should like to mention about development is that although we are looking forward to a fairer degree of economic development which would continue to offer our younger generation better opportunities for work, at the same time we are also looking at the quality of development that we want for our island. I do not think we are prepared to have development simply for the sake of development. We are also extremely concerned with the over-all environment of the island. We are becoming more and more aware of the fact that our geographical location puts us in a rather privileged position today. We realize that people from big cities envy us, and we would certainly want to try to avoid some of the mistakes they have made and perhaps belatedly regret. In other words, we are looking for a certain quality of development which will help us enjoy a reasonable standard of living but at the same time will help us keep and develop those environmental qualities which we still have and which have become so precious today.
In the agricultural sector, some of the programs related to the development plan helped island farmers enjoy a particularly good year in 1973. I am pleased to note that the Speech from the Throne speaks of a number of measures which will continue to help the farmer produce in greater quantity and quality so that we can achieve stabilization of food prices. In that respect I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has demonstrated great leadership and is moving in the right direction.
Island fishermen have also shared in this prosperity with good catches and increased earnings. The fishermen were extremely pleased with the compensation program for replacement of the gear they lost during a particularly severe storm. Some $617,000 was received by 845 fishermen on the island in compensation for their heavy losses. This was approximately two-thirds of the total losses, and the provincial government reimbursed the fishermen for the remainder.
Another very important fisheries development in P.E.I. is the^mall harbours development program. Results of the 1973-74 supplementary program can already be seen, and $335,000 was allocated to upgrade facilities at many of the island's small craft harbours. I am pleased to see that the Speech from the Throne refers to further "improvements in harbour facilities for fishing fleets." I think the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) have shown great understanding of the fishermen's needs in this regard.
Even before confederation transportation was a major problem in Prince Edward Island. One of the terms of confederation was that there would be a continuous link with the mainland. Because of this promise the federal government remains continually abreast of the problem of transportation. At the present time, two ice-breaker fer-
March 7, 1974

ries travel between Borden and Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick, in the winter, with four additional car ferries in the summer. This provides a superior year-round freight and passenger service between Wood Islands and Caribou, Nova Scotia. Planning is under way for more secure facilities at Wood Islands for the convenience of the travelling public, as well as improved berthing facilities. This construction should be completed by 1976. I am encouraged by the co-operative attitude of the Ministry of Transport in helping to alleviate transportation difficulties for islanders, and by the willingness to arrive at and ensure economic transportation access to markets in central and western Canada for island producers.
Turning to my Department of Veterans Affairs, I think I can say that we have had a most successful year from many points of view. The legislation enacted for Canada's veterans during the previous session of this parliament was far reaching and of vital importance. It incorporated some basic philosophies and principles which were proposed many years ago. It opened new doors for both veterans and their dependants to enjoy a richer and more secure way of life.
As hon. members are aware, there are three acts which govern the compensation paid to veterans and their dependants. These are the Pension Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act, and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. Last March, Bill C-148 was passed. It amended the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act so that they assumed a completely new profile. In effect, this bill changed the qualification requirements for allowances from a means-tested program to a limited income-tested program. This was done by removing the 'imitations covering personal property. In the same bill, the rates and ceilings were adjusted upwards, which resulted in a 25 per cent increase for the single recipient and a 28 per cent increase for the married recipient. Of course, these amounts continue to increase each year as a result of previous legislation which provided for automatic annual increases based on the consumer price index.
In his remarks a few days ago, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raised a question about the War Veterans Allowance Act, and particularly the fact that some veterans would be discriminated against. I simply wish to say to my hon. friend that every veteran in this country has received, and will continue to receive everything that is due him. Furthermore, I hope to be in a position very shortly to introduce legislation that will further amend the War Veterans Allowance Act so that benefits to veterans will be further enhanced.

Last June, the Pension Act was amended by the passage of Bill C-202. Under the Pension Act, pensions are awarded, as a matter of right, for death and disability related to military service in wartime. The bill provided an immediate increase of 24 per cent in the basic rate but, more importantly, it tied the rate to the average salary of a composite group of
The Address-Mr. D. J. MacDonald employees in the public service. Now, for the first time, the disability pension rate has achieved parity with the current cost of living standard. This was probably one of the most significant single advances in the history of Canadian veterans' legislation in more than 50 years and I think the veterans' organizations of this country deserve great credit for the very important ocntribution they made in the preparation of this legislation.
Another aspect of the whole pension system to veterans that I should mention very briefly is the question of backlog. As hon. members know, the legislation passed by this House in 1971 opened the door to a deluge of pension applications from veterans. This situation has created a considerable backlog with which the commission has been struggling ever since. I am happy to report that since last year that backlog has been considerably reduced. Whereas a year ago it was over 9,000 applications, it is now down to 7,300. What is more significant and encouraging is the fact that the monthly output of decisions has almost doubled since last year. I think the Canadian Pension Commission, together with the pension review board and the bureau of pensions advocates deserve great credit for this increased efficiency. I am sure this trend will continue and that in the not too distant future we will have eliminated that backlog.
On the subject of veterans' hospitals, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention that the government's policy of transferring hospitals to the jurisdiction of provinces is progressing quite well.

speechtext: Says who?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I say that. Three hospitals have already been transferred and negotiations are well under way for the transfer of a few more. I have no time to argue; the clock is moving too fast, Mr. Speaker. Although some people would like to see the veterans' hospitals remain as they are now, we certainly feel that it is in the best interest of veterans to proceed with these transfers. Otherwise, we run the risk of having to operate geriatric institutions within a short number of years and this is certainly not in the best interest of our veterans' population, not to mention the fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult, if not impossible, to find well qualified professionals to look after our veterans.
The year 1974 will mark two important events for the veterans of this country. As hon. members know, this coming June will be the thirtieth anniversary of the landing of the allied troops in northern France, which resulted in the liberation of Europe and the end of the second world war within one year. The government will certainly take a very active part in those celebrations, and I will be making an announcement very shortly concerning the participation of Canada in those ceremonies.
This year will also mark the twenty-fifth biennial national convention of the Royal Canadian Legion. This very important gathering will take place in St. John's, Newfoundland, during the first week of June. I do not think I need repeat here the important contributions made by the Royal Canadian Legion on behalf of all those who served their country in wartime.
Mr. Speaker, the Veterans Land Act has been a most successful post-war rehabilitation program and for that

In addition, some of the representations made have requested the reopening of the October 31, 1968, deadline for interested veterans to obtain a VLA certificate of qualification, that the loan ceiling for smallholding settlement purposes be increased and that the minimum acreage requirements be eliminated to enable veterans to purchase city-sized lots in urban areas. Notwithstanding the many occasions on which I have already done so, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is fundamental in the consideration of these requests to review the intent and purpose of the Veterans Land Act.

-programs enacted to assist veterans on their return to civilian life following wartime active service. Its purpose was to provide a measure of financial assistance to those veterans interested in settling on the land as full or part-time farmers, or in association with their occupation as commercial fishermen. For those veterans not interested in or who did not consider it practical to settle under the terms of the act, alternative benefits in the form of educational assistance or re-establishment credits were available.
I think it must be emphasized that the Veterans Land Act was a post-war rehabilitation measure and that almost 30 years have elapsed since the end of World War II, and 20 years in the case of the Korean conflict. I suggest it is difficult, within the normal sense of the words "rehabilitation in civilian life", to contend successfully that after these periods of time the words have any meaningful application. This is borne out by many of the individual letters I have received. Time and again reference is made to the fact that the veteran intends to retire in one, two, five or ten years' time and he would like to use the loan provisions of the act to acquire a retirement home. I am certain this was never contemplated when the legislation was enacted, nor when parliament gave unanimous consent in 1965 to the establishment of deadlines for phasing out VLA lending operations in a reasonable and orderly manner.
I stated earlier that, as the name implies, the Veterans Land Act was oriented toward agriculture to assist veterans interested in land utilization to acquire farmland for operation on a full or part-time farming basis. There is no question that the vast majority of the 130,000 veterans settled under those provisions of the act did utilize their properties for agricultural purposes, with the main body of those established as full-time farmers continuing to do so. This, however, is neither the purpose nor the indication today of veterans and others who want the act extended. Mr. Speaker, the desire today for an extension of VLA

lending operations coupled with an increase in the smallholding loan ceiling and elimination of the minimum acreage requirement is to provide assistance on favourable financial terms for the purchase of homes, including even condominium units, in urban areas.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Similar representations have been made throughout the 30 years that the Veterans Land Act has been in operation. On all occasions, and notwithstanding modifications made from time to time in the minimum size regulations, successive governments have recognized and adhered to the basic concept and purpose of the act. I strongly suggest that to do otherwise now would be grossly unfair to the many thousands of veterans who were not interested in, or found it impractical to live on a half-acre of land or more and made alternative, less favourable financial arrangements for the purchase of urban properties.
In the same connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind hon. members that on the recommendation of the Royal Canadian Legion part II of the Veterans Land Act was brought into being as far back as 1954 to provide assistance to those veterans interested in building their own homes on city-sized lots with National Housing Act mortgage financing. More than 4,500 veterans have used the provisions of part II in the 20 years they have been available.
It is acknowledged, of course, that the provision of suitable living accommodation necessarily has been an integral factor in the establishment of veterans under the Veterans-Land Act. Since the inception of operations, over 40,000 new homes have been constructed. This accomplishment has not, however, altered the fundamental purpose and orientation of the legislation, nor has it converted the program into a straight housing measure serving to duplicate or conflict with the provisions of the National Housing Act.
I remarked earlier that the Veterans Land Act was one of three alternative rehabilitation schemes. The university training program was concluded in the mid-fifties. The re-establishment credit benefits provided under the War Service Grants Act terminated October 31, 1968, which was also the final date for veterans interested in the possibility of settling under the Veterans Land Act to obtain a certificate of qualification. The periods in which these alternative benefits were available were considered to be adequate and appropriate, and it seems evident that the same opinion was held concerning the Veterans Land Act when in 1965 parliament gave unanimous approval to establishing March 31, 1974, as the final date for qualified veterans to submit loan applications for the purchase of properties.
Almost nine years have elapsed since that deadline was established. The terminal date has been well publicized. I am of the opinion, therefore, that veterans sincerely interested in obtaining VLA benefits for the purposes contemplated by the act have had ample time in which to do so. Virtually every veteran who obtained a VLA certificate of
March 7, 1974

qualification by the deadline of October 31, 1968, had already utilized the benefits alternative to those of the Veterans Land Act. In the circumstances, adherence to the lending deadline specified in the act will not represent a denial of benefits to any veteran.
On January 11 last, as reported at page 9281 of Hansard, I stated that if I had sufficient information to make me think the deadline date should be changed I would so recommend to the government. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I have carefully considered all relevant
The Address-Mr. D. J. Macdonald representations and data, including that determined by the Royal Canadian Legion in the survey it conducted last December. I am unable to conclude that such a recommendation would be warranted or appropriate.
